title: From Scaffolding to Ollauri
anecdote:
Luis Valentín and Carmen Enciso founded Valenciso in 1998 after 15 years working together in winery management. Their own project began without a permanent home: they made wine in rented facilities, first in Laguardia and then in San Vicente, with wine at one point split between Navarrete and Fuenmayor.

When they presented their wines to prospective UK importer Boutinot, scaffolding served as the tasting table, Valentín recalled in a 2018 interview. In 2006, they built their permanent winery in Ollauri, giving the project a home after those improvised beginnings.
identity_note: No vintage is identified. The importer identifies the documented 2012 release as 100% Tempranillo; neither that vintage nor an actual blend is established for this catalog entry. The story concerns the founders’ historical work, not current ownership.

title: A Family Cellar Looks Outward
anecdote:
Adega Eidos chose to professionalize its small family cellar around 2000, investing in technology and moving from Meaño to Padriñán in Sanxenxo. Its new winery opened in 2003, designed both to make wine and to let visitors follow the process.

In 2004, the estate joined an internationalization program while producing only about 20,000 bottles. Manager Marcelo Radio recalled that foreign markets would otherwise have been out of reach. That step developed into joint export activity with four other Galician wineries through Singular Galician Cellers.
identity_note: The abbreviated catalog name strongly favors Adega Eidos’s Eidos de Padriñán, but a label photograph is needed to confirm the release. Vintage is unknown; these are historical producer-level facts. Marcelo Radio is documented as manager, not winemaker.

title: A Second Selection
anecdote:
Paula Fandiño oversees the making of Mar de Frades Albariño, whose team selects healthy bunches in the vineyard, then brings them to the winery in small boxes for a second selection. She joined Mar de Frades as winemaker and managing director in 2007.

In one producer account, only 80% of the grapes advanced to maceration: the second selection excluded some of the harvested fruit before that stage. The winery also documented vineyard screening followed by a sorting table for its 2019 Albariño, without repeating that percentage.
identity_note: The catalog matches the standard Mar de Frades Albariño; vintage is unknown. The 80% figure describes one producer account, not a fixed annual rule or this unidentified vintage. Sources do not establish that Fandiño introduced the selection protocol.

title: Rebuilding Corton Grancey
anecdote:
The third Louis Latour bought Corton Grancey from the Grancey family in 1891, while phylloxera was devastating its vineyards. The purchase brought the château, winery and surrounding vines into the family estate, but two-thirds of those vineyards had been destroyed by the pest.

The Latour family subsequently replanted the vineyards—a recovery credited to the family collectively, rather than to Louis alone. The house now describes the restored property as the heart of Domaine Louis Latour, with Corton Grancey serving as the winery where its domaine wines are made and aged.
identity_note: Vintage unknown. The catalog does not distinguish plain Aloxe-Corton from the separately listed “Domaine Latour” version; neither is established as Premier Cru. This story is producer-level: the supplied evidence does not link this particular bottling to the vineyards acquired in 1891.

title: A Sorter’s Unexpected Sequel
anecdote:
Domaine Tollot-Beaut introduced optical sorting and a new destemmer for the 2014 harvest. Nathalie Tollot, part of the family team alongside cousins Olivier and Jean-Paul, credited the sorter with helping after a difficult growing season. She reported that the destemmer kept berries whole, releasing much less juice from broken fruit.

The following harvest brought an unexpected sequel: Nathalie said the optical sorter, bought only the year before, was unnecessary for the 2015 fruit. The estate had expanded its sorting capabilities, then encountered a harvest that did not need them.
identity_note: The catalog identifies the village-level Aloxe-Corton, not either separately named premier cru. Vintage is unknown. The equipment story is documented at estate level, not as the confirmed treatment of this cuvée or bottle.

title: Leasing Vineyards, Changing Grower Pay
anecdote:
IXSIR took long-term leases on entire vineyards, including existing plantings rather than only newly established sites. In a 2020 interview, Gabriel “Gabi” Rivero, then its chief winemaker and technical manager, described arrangements comparable to French fermage: a practical change in how the producer worked with growers.

Those growers had previously been paid by grape weight. Under IXSIR’s arrangements, the team reduced yields while growers earned more. Rivero presented the choice as putting quality ahead of volume, linking the vineyard decision to a documented improvement in grower income.
identity_note: Altitudes White is matched, but the catalog entry has no vintage. The lease story is producer-wide; no source ties those vineyards to this bottle. The catalog’s Bekaa Valley attribution remains unresolved because producer sources list multiple sites.

title: New Rows, Old Vines
anecdote:
Domaine Sigalas intensified its vineyard renewal from 2020, completing 17 hectares of new plantings by its September 2025 report. Vineyard manager Stratos Guillaume Xyrafis linked the work to declining productivity, drought and scarce, costly labor. The team kept traditional kouloura and kladeftiko training but planted new vines in rows to make cultivation more efficient.

In September 2026, some new plots yielded 3,000 kilograms per hectare, though Xyrafis cautioned that one or two years could not establish definitive results. Renewal also meant identifying viable old vines: systematically tended older vineyards maintained stable production that year.
identity_note: The catalog vintage is unknown; the 2022 technical sheet confirms the cuvée, not the bottle’s year. Sources do not establish that the renewed plots supplied this cuvée.

title: Apprenticeship Before the Cellar
anecdote:
Angelo Gaja joined the family estate in 1961, when it produced only Barbaresco. His father insisted that he learn vineyard work before entering the cellar. Angelo spent four years learning vine work and grafting under a demanding viticulture manager, while also studying economics and commerce.

He moved into cellar work in the late 1960s and began collaborating with oenologist Guido Rivella in 1970. Angelo described a partnership lasting 45 years, crediting Rivella’s production expertise with freeing him to concentrate more on the estate’s development and international markets.
identity_note: The catalog matches GAJA’s flagship Barbaresco, not a named single-vineyard bottling. Vintage is unknown; this historical producer story does not identify who made the catalog bottle.

title: From Family Grapes to Winery
anecdote:
Paolo Manzone and his wife, Luisella, founded their own agricultural business in 1999, renovating an old farmhouse at Meriame in Serralunga d’Alba. Paolo had worked as an enologist for other wineries; grapes from Luisella’s family vineyards had previously gone to a local cooperative.

The couple gave that family property a new role as the home of their winery. Their range later included San Giuliano Barbaresco, first produced in 2008 from Nebbiolo grown in Neive—a separate origin from the Meriame vineyards at the heart of their founding story.
identity_note: The catalogue identity is confirmed as Paolo Manzone Barbaresco DOCG San Giuliano. The bottle’s vintage is unknown; 2008 is the cuvée’s inaugural vintage, not an identification of this bottle.

title: A Father's Vines, Revisited
anecdote:
Luigi Pelissero replanted the upper Vanotu parcel in 1964, in Tre Stelle within the municipality of Barbaresco. His son Giorgio later chose fruit from the vineyard’s highest section, planted by his father, for the 2004 Vanotu Riserva, a bottling marking the winery’s fortieth anniversary.

The estate returned to those vines for Vanotu Riserva 2010, celebrating fifty years of the winery. Released in May 2020 after a ten-year project, it continued the link between Luigi’s replanting and the family’s commemorative wines: two anniversary releases rooted in the same vineyard intervention.
identity_note: The catalog identifies ordinary Pelissero Vanotu, not Riserva, and supplies no vintage. The commemorative Riserva releases are producer-and-vineyard context, not an identification of this bottle.

title: A Farmhouse of Their Own
anecdote:
Paolo Manzone joined his wife, Luisella, in establishing their own agricultural enterprise in 1999, after years working as a wine consultant. Their decision brought them to property already rooted in her family: the house and vineyards in Serralunga’s Meriame cru had belonged to Luisella’s family for generations.

The couple renovated an old farmhouse they owned in Serralunga, giving the venture its physical home. Today, the importer identifies Paolo and Luisella as the estate’s owners and operators. Fiorenza belongs to that estate’s range, though its Barbera grapes come from Sinio rather than Meriame.
identity_note: Producer and cuvée match. The importer identifies Fiorenza as Barbera d’Alba Superiore DOC; the catalog omits “Superiore,” unresolved without the bottle’s label. No vintage is specified. The 1999 founding story concerns the estate, not Fiorenza’s creation.

title: Piani Takes the Best Fruit
anecdote:
Giorgio Pelissero chose not to bottle the estate’s higher-tier Barbera Tulin in 2013. The third-generation winegrower and enologist had taken over the winery by 1990; this later decision is documented in Antonio Galloni’s December 2015 report, preserved in Pelissero’s press archive.

Instead, the best fruit went into Piani, changing the allocation between two distinct Barberas in the estate’s range that year. Pelissero identifies Piani hill in Ferrere, Treiso, as this cuvée’s site. The story is a specific instance of Giorgio directing fruit toward Piani rather than releasing a separate Tulin bottling.
identity_note: The catalog identifies Pelissero Barbera d’Alba DOC Piani but gives no vintage. The allocation decision described applies specifically to 2013, not necessarily to the unidentified bottle. The source does not explain why Giorgio withheld Tulin.

title: Half the Riserva, Held Back
anecdote:
Giacomo Borgogno & Figli chose to keep half its Barolo Riserva production rather than sell it, releasing those bottles only twenty years later. The estate’s dedicated collection account credits historical cellar leader Cesare Borgogno with beginning this practice in the 1920s.

That decision built a library of mature Riserva wines, with vintages reaching back to the 1960s. Borgogno describes the retention practice as continuing today: a long-running commitment to keeping bottles in its own cellars before release, rather than selling the entire Riserva production when first available.
identity_note: Producer story concerns Riserva, not the catalog’s standard Barolo. Vintage unknown; the photograph’s 2012 is not binding. The collection account credits Cesare, while the Italian timeline attributes the retention decision to Giacomo; the attribution is unresolved.

title: Choosing Verduno’s Collective Voice
anecdote:
Vittore Alessandria chose to replace Fratelli Alessandria’s Barolo classico with a bottling drawn exclusively from Verduno. The earlier blend had also included Gramolere fruit from Monforte d’Alba; his decision made the wine’s connection to his home village explicit. He described the intended expression as a choir, rather than the individual voice of Monvigliero.

Barolo del Comune di Verduno debuted with the 2017 vintage. The estate lists five contributing Verduno vineyards: Pisapola, Riva Rocca, Campasso, Rocche dell’Olmo and Boscatto—a concrete gathering of sites behind Vittore’s collective idea.
identity_note: The catalog matches this cuvée, but its vintage is unknown. 2017 identifies the inaugural release, not the catalog bottle.

title: Choosing a Foothold in Barolo
anecdote:
Giorgio Rivetti championed the potential of Grinzane Cavour as his siblings joined him in expanding La Spinetta into Barolo. After establishing their Barbaresco wines, the family acquired several hectares there, choosing to measure themselves against Piedmont’s established producers.

That investment connects to Garretti: La Spinetta identifies its vineyard in Grinzane Cavour and records 2001 as this Barolo’s first vintage. The estate also places Campè in the upper and central portions of the Garretti vineyard—a documented link between the sites, though the two bottlings remain distinct.
identity_note: The catalog identifies La Spinetta Barolo Garretti DOCG but supplies no vintage. The first-vintage date is historical, not the vintage of this bottle.

title: Adding Gianetto to the Family
anecdote:
Guido Porro acquired land in Gianetto in 2007, expanding the family estate beyond its established vineyard sites. The fourth generation, he had taken over from his father in 1996; the estate identifies him as both owner and oenologist.

That purchase brought a Gianetto Barolo into the estate’s lineup. In his March 2020 cellar-visit account, importer Anthony Lynch described Gianetto as a more recent addition, placed the vineyard opposite the Lazzarito hillside, and listed Porro’s 2015 bottling—a documented link between Guido’s expansion and this named cuvée.
identity_note: The catalog vintage is unknown. The cited 2015 release identifies the cuvée, not this entry’s vintage; the sources do not establish its first commercial vintage.

title: From Grapes to Their Own Wine
anecdote:
Paolo Manzone and his wife, Luisella, established their own agricultural business in 1999 and set about renovating an old farmhouse in Serralunga d’Alba. Luisella’s family had owned the Meriame house and vineyards for generations, but their grapes had been going to a local cooperative.

Paolo had worked as an oenologist for other wineries; the new estate gave him the opportunity to make wine from their own vineyards. A later milestone came with the 2008 harvest, when the estate introduced its Barolo Riserva, listed separately from its Meriame and Serralunga d’Alba Barolos.
identity_note: The catalog gives no vintage. The 2008 date identifies the Riserva’s first harvest, not the vintage of this bottle; the sources do not document why the cuvée was conceived.

title: From Micro-Cuvées to Serradenari
anecdote:
Giulia Negri returned to her family estate after completing her studies and travelling to Burgundy, then began learning winemaking and releasing small cuvées under her own name. It was a smaller start than taking charge of the entire estate from the outset.

In 2014, she took full responsibility for vineyard management and production. In her own account, Negri describes admiring independent, small-scale producers before choosing to commit herself to Serradenari’s vineyards and a team, with no opposition from her family. That estate makes the Barolo Serradenari.
identity_note: Vintage unknown. This producer-level story does not establish that Serradenari was among the initial micro-cuvées or identify its first vintage under Negri.

title: From Consulting to Their Own Wine
anecdote:
Paolo Manzone founded his own wine business in 1999, after years working as an oenologist for other companies. He and Luisella agreed to build on her family’s property in Serralunga, beginning renovations of an old farm. The house and Meriame vineyards had belonged to her family for generations; their grapes had previously been sold locally.

The producer records 1999 as the first harvest of its Barolo del Comune di Serralunga d’Alba. That gives this cuvée a documented place at the beginning of Paolo and Luisella’s venture, alongside their move from consulting and selling grapes toward making their own wine.
identity_note: The catalog matches Paolo Manzone’s Barolo DOCG Del Comune di Serralunga d’Alba. Vintage unknown: 1999 is the cuvée’s first harvest, not the catalog bottle’s vintage. The sources do not establish that this wine’s grapes came from Luisella’s inherited Meriame plots.

title: A Fresh Look at Rosé
anecdote:
Jean Roland-Billecart revisited rosé Champagne in the 1970s, aiming for a very pale colour when, according to the house’s history, rosé was still considered a secondary category. The fifth-generation family maker chose to give it renewed attention.

His cellar experiments had begun earlier: in 1958, he borrowed from traditional brewing to introduce longer, cooler fermentation and cold settling into the house’s tank vinification. Billecart-Salmon connects his later rosé project directly to Brut Rosé Non-Vintage, which it says went on to become its flagship cuvée.
identity_note: No vintage or release is identified. The archived Brut Rosé matches the catalog; the current Le Rosé page specifies Extra Brut, which should not be applied retrospectively. Jean is the historical maker in this story, not the current chef de cave, Florent Nys.

title: A Quicker Response in the Vines
anecdote:
Champagne Brice invested in two lightweight tracked vineyard vehicles after the difficult 2021 season exposed weaknesses in its move toward organic farming. Winemaker Christophe Constant recalled that herbicides had already been abandoned before his arrival in April 2019; the challenge was being able to act quickly when conditions demanded it.

The vehicles could work steep vineyards without compacting the soil, while weather-station monitoring helped the team respond. Jean-René Brice identified another practical requirement: keeping staff available through weekends. The estate’s change involved not just different treatments, but equipment and working schedules.
identity_note: Producer-level story, not evidence about this bottle’s farming or winemaker. The importer lists Héritage Brut Rosé; the current producer page says Extra-Brut, leaving the release unresolved. Neither lists Meunier. No vintage is established.

title: The Year Cerretalto Stayed Unbottled
anecdote:
Casanova di Neri chose not to release Cerretalto as a separate wine in 2014. An unusually cool, wet summer had made the harvest difficult, with conditions improving only toward the end of September. Tenuta Nuova was also withheld as a separate bottling.

Instead, grapes from both vineyards went into the estate’s Brunello di Montalcino Etichetta Bianca. Giacomo Neri was then sharing vineyard and winemaking responsibilities with his son Giovanni, who had joined in 2012; the estate’s history records the decision without crediting either man individually.
identity_note: The catalog vintage is unknown; this documented 2014 estate decision does not identify the listed wine’s vintage. Giacomo’s son Giovanni is distinct from his father, estate founder Giovanni Neri.

title: From Grapes to Her Own Brunello
anecdote:
Giovanna Neri built Col di Lamo after her father’s death in 1997, starting with land but no winery. In a 2020 interview with the Brunello producers’ consortium, she described the decisive change: instead of only selling grapes, she began making wine herself, initially in a friend’s garage in Torrenieri.

Neri bought equipment in 2000 and identified 2003 as her first Brunello vintage. Those steps took Col di Lamo from selling its grapes to producing its own Brunello—a beginning rooted in her decision to take on winemaking without a winery of her own.
identity_note: Producer and Brunello identity match. No vintage is specified, and the 1.5L format does not distinguish standard Brunello from the separately listed Limited Edition. The 2003 date describes the producer’s first Brunello vintage, not this bottle.

title: A Cellar Marked in Yellow
anecdote:
Altesino built modern cellars behind its vineyards, using a natural slope to create underground space for fermentation, maturation and bottling. The estate describes the investment as a way to improve and streamline production, with the underground setting providing insulation.

Elisabetta Gnudi Angelini added a personal detail to that working space: she chose yellow to decorate the large barrels. Her family has owned Altesino since 2002. Alongside the new facilities, the estate retained a section of the old cellar inside Palazzo Altesi for maturing its separate Brunello Montosoli bottling.
identity_note: The catalog identifies Altesino’s standard Brunello di Montalcino DOCG, not Montosoli or Riserva. No vintage is supplied; this producer-level story does not establish which cellar handled the cataloged wine.

title: Selecting Sangiovese at Greppo
anecdote:
Franco Biondi Santi worked on selecting Sangiovese at Tenuta Greppo in the 1970s. The estate credits its historical winemaker with the work that led to BBS11—Brunello Biondi Santi 11—a family-named clone formally recognized in 1978.

That selection went on to supply documented wines: the estate identifies BBS11 as the source for its 1994 Brunello and 2012 Riserva. The latter also closes the production period the estate attributes to Franco, which began with his first harvest in 1971: a vineyard project with a recorded place in his winemaking career.
identity_note: The producer is Biondi-Santi, Tenuta Greppo. No vintage is specified, and regular Brunello versus Riserva is unresolved. These historical examples do not establish this bottle’s clone or winemaker.

title: A Brunello Without a Riserva
anecdote:
Francesco Ripaccioli chose not to make a Riserva at Canalicchio di Sopra in 2020 because he was not convinced it was the right choice. He belongs to the third-generation family team, alongside Marco and Simonetta, whose involvement at the estate began in 2001.

According to journalist Michael Godel’s report, all the fruit from Vigna Vecchia Mercatale went into the regular 2020 Brunello instead. Yet this did not produce an unusually large release: overall production was below 2019, even with the fruit redirected from the unmade Riserva.
identity_note: The catalog matches the regular Brunello di Montalcino, but gives no vintage. This 2020-specific allocation story illustrates the producer’s work, not necessarily the production history of the unidentified bottle. Francesco is part of the family team, not the sole maker.

title: Rebuilding Casanova Around Sangiovese
anecdote:
Giovanni Neri bought Podere Casanova in May 1971 and renamed it Casanova di Neri. On this roughly 200-hectare farm east of Montalcino, wine had been a marginal activity, mostly sold in bulk. With help from local producers, he restored existing Sangiovese vineyards and planted new ones.

In 1978, the estate produced its first Brunello, selecting grapes from three vineyards in northeastern Montalcino. The estate traces its White Label lineage to that wine: a documented outcome of the founder’s vineyard rebuilding, before his son Giacomo took over in 1991.
identity_note: Producer confirmed; the abbreviated catalog name does not identify White Label or another specific Brunello bottling. Vintage is unspecified. This is producer history, not a claim about the catalog bottle’s vineyard origins.

title: Renewal Alongside the Original Vines
anecdote:
Filippo Chia began renewing Castello Romitorio’s wines and winemaking approach in the mid-2000s, focusing on single-variety Sangiovese. His arrival coincided with a new cellar, and the estate credits him with developing new Sangiovese vineyards: an expansion of the property his father, Sandro, founded in 1984.

That renewal did not replace the founding vineyards. The estate says Sandro’s original plantings still account for approximately half its vineyards. The standard Brunello’s own page describes both old and new Sangiovese vineyards, connecting this bottling to a producer whose development has retained a substantial part of its beginnings.
identity_note: The catalog matches the standard Brunello di Montalcino DOCG, not Riserva or Filo di Seta. Vintage is unknown. Estate pages date Filippo’s transition differently, to 2005 and 2006; no formal head-winemaker title or responsibility for this unspecified vintage is established.

title: From Grapes to First Brunello
anecdote:
Giovanna Neri began building Col di Lamo in 1997 with land but no cellar. A law graduate, she initially sold her grapes before beginning to make wine in a friend’s garage in Torrenieri—a modest starting point for her move from grape grower to independent wine producer.

She bought winemaking equipment in 2000 and identifies 2003 as the year of her first Brunello di Montalcino. Today, the estate says Giovanna personally directs every stage of production, supported by her daughter Diletta: a second generation now involved in the estate she built.
identity_note: The catalog most likely identifies the standard Brunello, but Col di Lamo makes several distinct Brunellos; the bottling remains provisional without a label or fuller record. Vintage unknown. This story concerns the producer’s development, not the unidentified vintage.

title: A Dinner, Then a Rebuilding
anecdote:
Gianni Maccari met Ridolfi owner Giuseppe Valter Peretti by chance at a dinner with friends in 2012. By 2014, they were working together to rebuild the estate, with Maccari serving as winemaker and estate director after experience at Poggio di Sotto.

Maccari made healthy vineyards a priority, crediting Giulio Gambelli for that principle. He recalled replacing clones he considered too focused on productivity. Alongside that vineyard work, Ridolfi completely renovated its cellar in 2014, expanding capacity while preserving the historic hamlet’s original configuration.

title: Testing New Ground
anecdote:
Casanova di Neri began Tenuta Nuova by studying microclimates and exposures before planting Sangiovese on ground where, in the estate’s account, the variety had never grown. The team also investigated clones, rootstocks, cultivation practices and planting density: a series of decisions behind this particular Brunello.

The project reached its first harvest in autumn 1993 at Le Cetine, marking the estate’s first move into the southern part of the appellation. Giacomo Neri had taken over the business in 1991, so Tenuta Nuova’s first crop arrived during his leadership.

title: Keeping Fruit for Snowden
anecdote:
Scott and Randy Snowden replanted the main vineyard in 1981 with budwood from Jordan Vineyards. The brothers had taken over management of the ranch after their father Wayne died in 1977, and spent the following decade supplying fruit to Stag’s Leap Wine Cellars.

In 1993, they chose to keep enough grapes to make 383 cases under the Snowden label; the share retained for their own wines later increased. The family’s next generation entered the cellar when Diana Snowden Seysses became winemaker with the 2005 harvest.
identity_note: The catalog’s “Brother’s Vineyard” matches Snowden’s official “Brothers Vineyard.” Vintage is unknown; neither the 2023 source listing nor the supplied reference to 2013 identifies this bottle’s vintage.

title: From Family Farm to Caymus
anecdote:
Chuck Wagner agreed at 19 to join his parents, Charlie and Lorna, in turning their farming and home-winemaking operation into a commercial winery. They believed selling their own wine could provide a better living; together, they founded Caymus in 1972.

The work began before the winery opened: from November 1971 to mid-March 1972, Chuck, his father and one other worker pruned 55 acres. That spring they built the 3,200-square-foot winery. Caymus opened with 240 cases of Cabernet Sauvignon—a concrete beginning to the family’s commercial venture.
identity_note: Best match: Caymus Vineyards Napa Valley Cabernet Sauvignon, distinct from Special Selection and California Cabernet Sauvignon; a bottle label would confirm the abbreviated identity. title: From Internship to Leadership
anecdote:
Elizabeth Vianna accepted an internship at Chimney Rock after her friend and former schoolmate Leilah Backhus, then assistant winemaker, encouraged her to join. Vianna already knew she wanted to make Cabernet Sauvignon. At the estate, she worked with winemaker Doug Fletcher, who became her mentor.

She returned as assistant winemaker in 2002 and became head winemaker in 2005, when Fletcher moved into broader oversight of the Terlato properties. Fletcher remained closely involved in vineyard farming while Vianna handled winemaking, turning an apprenticeship into a leadership succession.
identity_note: The catalog identifies Chimney Rock and Cabernet Sauvignon, but not a definitive cuvée or vintage. This is producer-level history, not an attribution of this undated bottle to Vianna.

title: Redrawing the Vineyard Map
anecdote:
Faust winemaker David Jelinek and estate director Jen Beloz redrew management blocks at the Coombsville estate after repeated vineyard walks revealed uneven ripening and recurring water stress. Combining those observations with technical data, the team mapped irregular shapes instead of treating conventional rows as uniform units.

Over six years of refinement, they adjusted selected trellising and installed irrigation where moisture tracking indicated a need, aiming to narrow ripeness differences at harvest. In the cellar, small vineyard lots stayed separate in numerous small tanks, allowing individual fermentation decisions before blend selection.
identity_note: The catalog matches Faust Napa Valley Cabernet Sauvignon, not The Pact. The detailed vineyard account concerns The Pact, so this is a producer-level story, not a production claim for the cataloged wine. No vintage is supplied.

title: A Handover Between Friends
anecdote:
To Kalon Vineyard Company brought Tony Biagi into a collaborative handover with Andy Erickson: friends for more than 25 years, the two worked together to finalize the producer’s 2022 blends rather than drawing an immediate line between their tenures.

The producer describes 2023 as Biagi’s opportunity to take the lead after that shared work. Its winemaker timeline records Erickson for 2016–2022 and Biagi from 2022 onward; the overlapping dates reflect their collaboration. The 2021 Highest Beauty record credits Erickson directly as this cuvée’s winemaker.
identity_note: The catalog names no vintage, so this bottle cannot be assigned to either winemaker. Joint work on the producer’s 2022 blends does not establish individual contributions to 2022 Highest Beauty.

title: From Harvest Intern to Winemaker
anecdote:
Ashley Hepworth joined Joseph Phelps for the 1999 harvest as an intern, hired personally by Joe Phelps. She stayed beyond that first season, progressing through laboratory technician and enologist roles before becoming associate winemaker in 2004.

In October 2008, Hepworth was promoted to winemaker, taking responsibility for day-to-day production of the estate’s Napa Valley wines. By the 2022 harvest, she was still working with and learning from people she had met more than twenty years earlier—a career built within the team she first joined as an intern.
identity_note: Probable match to Joseph Phelps Vineyards Napa Valley Cabernet Sauvignon, not the separate Backus Vineyard bottling. No vintage is specified; this producer-level story does not establish Hepworth as the maker of this particular bottle or identify its fruit sourcing.

title: From Planting to Partnership
anecdote:
Jayson Pahlmeyer joined his friend John Caldwell in 1981 to plant Bordeaux vine material on Caldwell’s Coombsville property. According to the estate’s history, the cuttings had been brought clandestinely from Bordeaux. Their planting project would become the starting point for a winemaking partnership.

The vineyard attracted Randy Dunn, who agreed to make Pahlmeyer’s first wine in exchange for access to its fruit. That arrangement produced the 1986 Pahlmeyer Proprietary Red: Pahlmeyer was the founder and planting collaborator, while Dunn was the winemaker responsible for the debut.
identity_note: Producer history only. The catalog does not distinguish Jayson Cabernet Sauvignon from Pahlmeyer Pièce de Résistance; vintage is unknown. The historical Proprietary Red is not an identification of this bottle.

title: Two Tons to Begin
anecdote:
Dave Phinney took a temporary harvest job at Robert Mondavi in 1997, a year after a semester studying in Florence immersed him in wine. Orin Swift’s account connects that harvest experience with his decision to make wine of his own.

In 1998, he established Orin Swift Cellars with two tons of Zinfandel: the concrete beginning of the estate that produces Palermo. The winery identifies Phinney as its founder, winemaker and creative director, giving him a continuing role beyond the founding chapter of the business.
identity_note: The catalog identifies Palermo, Orin Swift’s Napa Valley Cabernet Sauvignon. Vintage is unknown; the 2016 archive verifies the cuvée, not this listing’s year. The founding story concerns the producer, not Palermo’s creation.

title: Rebuilding Around Cabernet
anecdote:
Silver Oak rebuilt its Oakville winery after a fire destroyed the historic facility in 2006. Faced with salvaging the building or starting afresh, second-generation proprietor David R. Duncan recognized an opportunity to create a winery specifically suited to Silver Oak’s Cabernet production.

The winemaking team reconsidered the building’s orientation, crush-pad location, fermentation-room workflow, barrel-washing equipment, and tank sizes and placement. In 2016, the rebuilt Napa Valley winery achieved LEED Platinum certification for existing buildings, operations and maintenance—a documented outcome of the rebuilding effort at the facility that produces its Napa Valley Cabernet Sauvignon.
identity_note: The supplied region identifies the Napa Valley bottling, not Alexander Valley. No vintage is supplied, so this bottle cannot be placed before or after the rebuild or assigned to a winemaker’s tenure. David R. Duncan’s role here was proprietor, not winemaker.

title: From Wine Service to Cellar
anecdote:
Nick Moraida changed course from wine sales and restaurant work to studying winemaking at Fresno State. He had intended to become a sommelier and wine director, but a friend’s invitation to pick grapes and make a project wine gave him the experience of taking a wine from beginning to end.

At Sinegal Estate, Moraida worked as intern, cellar master, enologist, associate winemaker and winemaker before the estate announced his appointment as Director of Winemaking—a progression through the production team over the preceding eight years.
identity_note: The catalog matches Sinegal Estate’s Napa Valley Cabernet Sauvignon, but no vintage is supplied, so this bottle cannot be attributed to Moraida. The winery lists both Moraida and Alanna Robinson as Director of Winemaking; succession timing is unclear.

title: Keeping the Parcels Apart
anecdote:
Vasse Felix’s cellar team fermented individual vineyard sections separately for its 2008 Cabernet Sauvignon, selecting batches before making the final blend. That work fell within Virginia Willcock’s tenure as Chief Winemaker, which began in October 2006. Keeping those sections apart became a thread in the Cabernet’s documented cellar experiments.

In 2016, individual sections fermented with indigenous yeasts, while a small Petit Verdot component underwent carbonic maceration before whole-bunch fermentation. By 2022, the team’s Cabernet trials included an open oak vat, a concrete egg and a cocciopesto vessel alongside stainless steel.
identity_note: The best match is the Premier Cabernet Sauvignon, distinct from Filius and Tom Cullity; a label photograph would confirm the tier. No vintage is supplied, so these dated practices cannot be assigned to the catalog bottle. Sources do not establish who personally proposed each trial.

title: Two Harvests, One Continuing Experiment
anecdote:
Chris Howell and Cain’s cellar team turned a difficult harvest into a lasting blending practice. In cold, wet 1998, they found that wine from 1997 complemented the new lots. Friends in Bordeaux had encouraged Howell to consider blending across vintages; the experiment became part of Cain Cuvée’s production.

Cain continued combining two harvests in varying proportions, rather than maintaining a continuously replenished solera reserve. NV14 carries that practice forward: its producer’s technical sheet identifies 2013 and 2014 as the contributing harvests and records its release on September 1, 2018.
identity_note: NV14 is a multi-vintage release designation, not a single 2014 vintage. The sources establish the Cuvée program’s origin and NV14’s continuation of it, not a separate NV14-specific blending anecdote.

title: Experimentation, Then a Narrower Focus
anecdote:
Giovanni Manetti experimented with Syrah and other international varieties at Fontodi in the 1980s. Having become involved after his family moved there in 1979, he gradually took on responsibility, working hands-on in the vineyards rather than directing the estate only from a distance.

Manetti later removed many international-variety vines to concentrate on Sangiovese, which he said occupied 95% of the planted vineyard area by 2018. Fontodi nevertheless lists Case Via Syrah as a distinct wine from the Case Via and Pecille vineyards; the sources do not explain why this Syrah was retained.
identity_note: Matched to Fontodi Case Via Syrah, Colli Toscana Centrale IGT. Vintage unknown. The sources do not establish the cuvée’s planting date, uninterrupted parcel history, or who made the unidentified vintage.

title: The Harvest That Became a Career
anecdote:
María Vargas joined Marqués de Murrieta for the 1995 harvest as a student and stayed. In her account, staying did not mean standing still: new winery, wine and vineyard projects kept giving her work to pursue. She recalled initially feeling unsure of her place among the cellar workers she admired.

From assistant winemaker, Vargas rose to the leading winemaking position in 2000. Today, the estate names her as technical director and leader of its winemaking team on the official Castillo Ygay page—a career that began with that student harvest.
identity_note: Producer-level story: no vintage is supplied, so Vargas’s responsibility for this particular bottle cannot be established. The official page’s featured 2012 is not assigned to this catalog record.

title: A Handover, Then a Farming Change
anecdote:
Richard Rottiers and Amandine Marchive took over Domaine des Malandes from their mother, Lyne Marchive, in 2018. Richard heads the domaine, while Amandine handles sales and communications. The siblings initiated organic conversion in 2019, making a change in vineyard practice part of their stewardship.

The estate’s technical presentation for its 2019 Fourchaume Vieilles Vignes records an earlier step: chemical weed control had stopped in 2018. It also documents organic fertilizer and crop protection during conversion, giving a concrete account of the farming changes alongside the family handover.
identity_note: The catalog matches Domaine des Malandes Fourchaume, but specifies neither vintage nor Vieilles Vignes. The technical evidence concerns 2019 Fourchaume Vieilles Vignes; it does not establish the farming or certification status of the unidentified catalog vintage.

title: A Cellar Built Around Gravity
anecdote:
Domaine de l’Enclos built its partly underground cellar in 2016, the year it first vinified a vintage on-site. Brothers Romain and Damien Bouchard work the vineyards and make the wines with their team; the new winery gave that work a gravity-flow layout.

Grapes are sorted on a vibrating table and pneumatically pressed before the juice flows by gravity into stainless-steel tanks in the 450-square-meter, temperature-controlled underground cellar. Alongside this infrastructure, the brothers use indigenous yeasts for fermentation and make their wines without fining or cold treatment.
identity_note: Probable producer match, not conclusive. The catalog’s “Les Fourchaumes” does not exactly match the official La Fourchaume or separate La Fourchaume Dédé bottlings. This story is producer-scoped; the exact cuvée and vintage remain unresolved.

title: Two Hectares of Change
anecdote:
Didier Séguier introduced grass cover on two hectares at William Fèvre in spring 1999. He had arrived the previous September and recalled being troubled that herbicides had stripped vegetation even from the vineyard banks. His first intervention was a small trial, not an estate-wide conversion.

The estate later documented a broader shift: two-thirds of its vineyards had been cultivated organically since 2006, with biodynamic methods introduced in 2010. In May 2015, William Fèvre announced High Environmental Value certification, assessing areas including biodiversity, plant-health strategy and fertilizer management.
identity_note: Producer identity is supported, but the exact Chablis bottling and vintage are unknown. These estate-level practices cannot be attributed to this bottle or its grapes. High Environmental Value certification is not organic certification.

title: A Native Start, Then Reassurance
anecdote:
Stephanie Jacobs began using native yeasts to start fermentation of Cakebread Cellars’ signature Chardonnay. In a December 2021/January 2022 interview, she described that change; Cakebread’s 2019 technical sheet credits her as winemaker for its standard Napa Valley Chardonnay, placing her directly behind that bottling during this period.

Jacobs did not leave the whole fermentation to native yeast. Halfway through, she added commercial yeast for reassurance that fermentation would finish. Her Chardonnay protocol paired a native start with a deliberate safeguard, rather than leaving native yeast to carry fermentation through to completion.
identity_note: The catalog does not conclusively distinguish standard Chardonnay from Chardonnay Reserve, and vintage is unknown. This is a historical producer-level account, not a protocol established for this bottle; Jacobs is not identified as the current winemaker.

title: Seven Days for Chardonnay
anecdote:
Chateau Montelena compressed its 2020 Napa Valley Chardonnay harvest from the usual 15–30 days into one week. Heat and a smaller crop brought the vineyards toward ripeness together, rather than in sequence, testing the adaptable team, equipment and working methods described by winemaker Matt Crafton.

Picking began on August 22 and finished on August 28, bringing in the entire Chardonnay crop in the winery’s fastest Chardonnay harvest on record at the time. Crafton credited the team’s dedication and expertise for completing the accelerated harvest successfully.
identity_note: The catalog matches Chateau Montelena Napa Valley Chardonnay, but supplies no vintage. This documented 2020 episode is presented at producer scope, not as the harvest history of the unidentified bottle.

title: A Partnership, Then a Handover
anecdote:
Hope Goldie joined Darioush as enologist in 2005, became assistant winemaker in 2007 and winemaker in 2012. Her progression unfolded alongside founding winemaker Steve Devitt, with whom she worked for nearly fifteen years before the winery announced her promotion to Director of Winemaking in January 2020.

At that handover, Devitt became Director of Viticulture, taking responsibility for vineyard management and grower relations while Goldie led winemaking. Darioush’s 2022 Signature Chardonnay technical sheet subsequently credited Goldie as winemaker, documenting her connection to that cuvée after the leadership transition.
identity_note: Producer-level history: the catalog omits “Signature,” so the exact cuvée is unconfirmed, and no vintage is specified. Goldie’s documented Chardonnay credits do not establish who made this bottle. Trevor Durling subsequently succeeded her in winemaking leadership.

title: Securing Chardonnay’s Vineyard Roots
anecdote:
Miljenko “Mike” Grgich bought 88 acres in Los Carneros in 1989, choosing southern Napa’s cooler conditions for Chardonnay. The founding winemaker of Grgich Hills wanted to own the source of his grapes; after the Carneros vineyard’s success, he bought the American Canyon property in 1996 to expand Chardonnay production.

By 2005, the producer had acquired enough vineyard land to supply all its grapes from its own holdings. That shift reached the label: “Estate” was added, and in 2007 the winery formally became Grgich Hills Estate.
identity_note: The producer is verified, but the catalog establishes neither tier nor vintage. This story concerns producer history, not the sourcing or winemaking of the unidentified bottle.

title: A Night Shift Toward Independence
anecdote:
Dave Phinney took a temporary harvest job at Robert Mondavi in 1997, accepting the available night shift, from 3:30 p.m. to 1 a.m. He learned practical cellar work from the crew and decided that, if he was going to work that hard, he wanted eventually to work for himself.

He founded Orin Swift the following year, starting with two tons of Zinfandel. But the difficult 1998 season became a lesson in the limits of fixing problems in the cellar: Phinney released no wine from that first attempt, and the estate’s timeline records its first wine as a failure.
identity_note: Producer-level story. The catalog lists Napa Valley, but Orin Swift identifies Mannequin as California Chardonnay sourced across appellations. No vintage is specified; the supplied 2020 technical sheet does not establish the catalog bottle’s vintage.

title: A Vineyard Built Together
anecdote:
Eric Jensen, My Favorite Neighbor’s founder and farmer-winemaker, encouraged Lynn and O’Neal Gray to plant a vineyard at their farm. The Grays had not planned to grow grapes, but Jensen was seeking more fruit sources for MFN and helped them establish MoonSprings Vineyard from the ground up.

Planting began in 2018, and the Grays developed an extensive set of vineyard practices. MoonSprings went on to become an MFN partner vineyard and a named vineyard-designate bottling, giving the collaboration a lasting place in the producer’s range.
identity_note: Matched to My Favorite Neighbor Chardonnay; Booker is an associated but distinct brand. Vintage is unknown. title: An Internship, Then a Return
anecdote:
Johannes Scheid approached Walter Schug after a presentation at Germany’s Geisenheim University and asked for a harvest internship. Schug hired him on the spot for the 2009 harvest—a first placement at the winery where Scheid would later become winemaker.

Scheid returned for a full year in 2011–2012, then worked abroad and became production manager at Benziger in 2015. In 2016, he chose to return to Schug as assistant winemaker. Today, the estate identifies him as winemaker, with responsibility for its Pinot Noir and Chardonnay production.
identity_note: Producer identity is supported, but the catalog establishes neither the Chardonnay tier nor a vintage. The 2021 Carneros technical sheet is identity evidence only. This producer-level story does not assign Scheid to the particular bottle.

title: A Successor From Within
anecdote:
Émilien Érard joined Charles Heidsieck in 2018, building experience in winery management and relations with the growers and cooperatives supplying the house. His preparation also took him into blending: the producer credits him with seven years on its tasting committee, participating in the blends.

When Élise Losfelt chose to leave for her family estate, Château de l’Engarran in Languedoc, Charles Heidsieck promoted Érard to Chef de Caves. The appointment placed someone already involved in both its supply relationships and cellar decisions at the head of the house’s winemaking.
identity_note: The catalog matches Charles Heidsieck Rosé Réserve, not its separate vintage rosé. No vintage or release is identified, so the cellar master responsible for this bottle’s original blend cannot be established. The succession story is producer-level.

title: Investment and a Shared Cellar Team
anecdote:
Alexandre de Malet Roquefort purchased Château Armens, then invested in modernizing its vinification and refining the wine’s maturation. The producer documents a program of cellar improvements, rather than specific equipment purchases: the story here begins with an owner committing resources to how Armens was made and aged.

In a July 2024 interview, Alexandre identified the people behind that work: Château La Gaffelière’s team makes and vinifies Château Armens. He also described Armens as integrated into the family’s estate group, connecting his investment with a production team shared across the family properties.
identity_note: Vintage unknown. The purchase date differs between sources: the producer gives 1999; Alexandre’s interview gives 1998. Alexandre is verified as purchaser and owner, not individual cellar winemaker. The production-team attribution is documented in 2024.

title: New Team, Separate Identity
anecdote:
Ronan and Monique Laborde took over Lécuyer’s operating company in 2022, choosing to keep the estate distinct from their Château Clinet. The transaction transferred the company Petit-Lecuyer, not the vineyard land: the vines remained with an investment group of approximately 100 shareholders.

The Labordes announced that the two properties would coexist separately, each retaining its own terroir. Lécuyer would continue through traditional distribution with support from Clinet’s commercial partners. Its distributor now identifies Château Clinet’s team as responsible for producing and bottling Lécuyer—a change in stewardship without merging the estates.
identity_note: Château l’Ecuyer matches Château Lécuyer. Vintage unspecified, so this producer-level account does not assign the bottle to either maker era. The catalog’s Cabernet Sauvignon/Merlot description remains unresolved: the 2017 sheet lists Merlot and Cabernet Franc for that vintage only.

title: A New Cellar Tested
anecdote:
Château La Gaffelière’s team put its brand-new vat room to work during the difficult 2013 harvest. A cold, wet spring had delayed vine development by nearly three weeks, while damp conditions late in the season brought a threat of botrytis. The estate credits its technicians’ work in both vineyard and cellar.

Their response combined careful vineyard sorting with optical sorting at reception, restrained extraction and low fermentation temperatures. Parcels were vinified separately in temperature-controlled tanks filled by gravity: a documented account of how the team handled that challenging year.
identity_note: The catalog identifies the estate’s first wine, not Clos La Gaffelière. Vintage is unknown; this 2013 producer story does not date the bottle. The incomplete historical classification wording cannot establish its designation; the estate withdrew from the 2022 classification process. The catalog’s grape shorthand remains unverified: current estate material names Merlot and Cabernet Franc, while its 2005 archive also records Cabernet Sauvignon.

title: The Decision to Wait
anecdote:
Château Margaux’s team chose to wait after heavy September rain in 2017, rather than pick red grapes before sufficient ripeness. With possible Botrytis damage weighing against the risk of harvesting too early, optimistic weather forecasts encouraged the team to hold off.

Red-grape picking then ran from September 12 to October 3 in conditions the estate describes as exceptionally fine. In its account of the 2017 Grand Vin, Château Margaux reports that later tastings reassured the team about its decision to delay: a documented outcome of that particular harvest gamble.
identity_note: The catalog gives no vintage. This producer-scope story concerns the documented 2017 Grand Vin harvest, not necessarily the cataloged bottle; the decision is attributed to the team, not to Philippe Bascaules individually.

title: Built Parcel by Parcel
anecdote:
Régis Bernaleau expanded Château Mongravey from two hectares he inherited in 1981, buying additional vineyard parcels around Arsac. That parcel-by-parcel growth built an estate now covering 12 hectares, with 29 vineyard parcels spread across several separate blocks rather than one continuous holding.

The next chapter belongs to the family’s division of work. Régis is identified as the founder, while his son Jérôme is responsible for production and Karin Bernaleau handles commercialization and communication. The estate presents this as a family undertaking being passed to the next generation.
identity_note: The catalog matches Château Mongravey, not the separately listed Mongravey Cuvée Margaux. Vintage is unknown; neither Supérieur nor Exceptionnel can be assigned from the catalog wording. This estate-level story does not identify who made the unspecified vintage.

title: Thirty Years Rebuilding Romassan
anecdote:
The Ott family acquired Château Romassan in 1956 and began a vineyard reconstruction that took 30 years. They replanted the vineyards completely, reorganizing and levelling the small plots to establish terraced and espalier vineyards. It was a sustained rebuilding of the estate that makes Château Romassan Rosé, rather than a change confined to one cuvée.

Today, Romassan’s estate account still describes vineyards planted on terraces and restanques, supplying both its rosé and red wines. The work continued beyond the vineyard: the estate records a cellar modernization in 2023.
identity_note: The catalog identifies Château Romassan Rosé, AOC Bandol, by Domaines Ott; vintage is unknown. This estate-level story is not attributed to current cellar master Estelle Mazoire, whose involvement in the historical reconstruction or 2023 modernization is not established.

title: Keeping the Commitment, Changing the Work
anecdote:
Sophie and Catherine Armenier took over Domaine de Marcoux in 1995 and kept the organic and biodynamic approach their brother Philippe had introduced estate-wide in 1991. Sophie handled winemaking; Catherine worked mainly in the vineyards. In a later interview, they recalled persisting through difficult early vintages and professional skepticism.

Sophie’s son Vincent Estevenin joined in 2014. He describes an evolving vineyard routine: less ploughing, sheep grazing in winter and replanted boundary hedges. The estate also reports Ecocert oversight of organic cultivation since 1991, distinguishing that certification from its use of biodynamic preparations.
identity_note: Vintage unknown. Identification as the standard Châteauneuf-du-Pape Rouge, rather than Vieilles Vignes, is provisional pending a bottle label; the story concerns estate-wide practices.

title: Sisters Divide the Work
anecdote:
Sophie and Catherine Armenier took over Domaine de Marcoux in 1995, dividing responsibility between cellar and vineyard. Sophie led vinification; Catherine concentrated on growing the grapes. The estate’s history places their handover in a period when women’s place at the head of a wine estate was not straightforward.

The next generation joined before that partnership ended: Sophie’s son, Vincent Estevenin, arrived in 2014 to work alongside his mother and aunt. Catherine retired in 2019, giving the family five years of overlap before another change in the estate’s team.
identity_note: The estate confirms the exact Vieilles Vignes cuvée. No vintage is supplied; this producer-level history does not identify the team responsible for a particular bottle.

title: An Experiment Earns Its Own Bottle
anecdote:
Castello di Ama appointed Marco Pallanti to lead its winemaking in 1982. After his arrival, the estate tested nontraditional varieties alongside Sangiovese, including a trial that grafted Merlot onto a small existing parcel of Canaiolo and Malvasia Bianca. It was an estate experiment, not a decision attributed to Pallanti alone.

The results persuaded the estate to give the experiment a separate bottling rather than retain it only for blending. That wine became L’Apparita, with its first vintage in 1985—a distinct outcome of the producer’s early trials.
identity_note: The catalog matches Castello di Ama San Lorenzo, Chianti Classico Gran Selezione DOCG; vintage unknown. This is a producer-level story: the sources do not establish that the experimental parcel supplies San Lorenzo.

title: A Blending Trial Becomes L’Apparita
anecdote:
Marco Pallanti took charge of winemaking at Castello di Ama in 1982. During his first three years, a small parcel was grafted to Merlot as the estate tested nontraditional varieties as potential partners for Sangiovese. The vines replaced Canaiolo and Malvasia Bianca.

The experiment gained a separate identity rather than remaining solely a source for blends: in 1985, Castello di Ama first produced L’Apparita as a varietal Merlot. This is a chapter in Montebuoni’s producer’s history, documenting how an early trial became another wine in the estate’s portfolio.
identity_note: The producer identifies Montebuoni as Chianti Classico Riserva DOCG; the catalog omits Riserva. This bottle’s vintage is unknown. Montebuoni debuted in 2018; no causal link to the Merlot experiment is established.

title: Three Cellars, One Estate
anecdote:
Castello di Volpaia’s owning family brought three separate fermentation cellars into one operation. Giovannella Stianti recalled that, before her father bought the property, three families worked independently, each with different vessels: wood, concrete or enamelled iron. Unifying them was part of the estate’s redevelopment.

The work extended beyond the cellars: Giovannella said the family paid to bury electrical cables throughout the village. Her daughter Federica described the resulting arrangement, with cellars and barrel rooms housed inside medieval buildings that appear domestic—a wine-producing estate woven into the village itself.
identity_note: Matched to Castello di Volpaia Chianti Classico Riserva DOCG. Vintage unknown. The cellar redevelopment concerns the producer overall, not a documented method for this cuvée.

title: A Team’s Organic Transition
anecdote:
Domaine Charles Joguet commissioned René Morlat of INRA Angers to study its vineyard parcels in 2004, helping prepare a move toward organic farming. Kevin Fontaine joined in 2006 with responsibility for vineyards and vinification, as the estate began changing soil cultivation and canopy management.

The domaine also trained its vineyard team in a new approach to support the transition: this was a collective undertaking during Fontaine’s tenure, not his alone. Formal engagement with Ecocert followed in 2013, and 2016 became the estate’s first officially certified organic vintage.
identity_note: The catalog vintage is unknown; the 2024 Rosé listing confirms identity but cannot establish this bottle’s organic certification. Charles Joguet retired from wine production in 1997; he is not the current winemaker.

title: One Plot Earns Its Own Wine
anecdote:
Franc Petit began replanting the vineyards and olive orchards after acquiring Domaine de l’Abbaye. According to a 2016 account, he came to regard the replanted Clos Beylesse parcel as the source of his best grapes and chose to bottle a wine exclusively from that plot.

That parcel-by-parcel decision grew into something larger: the same account reports that Clos Beylesse eventually represented most of the estate’s wine production. It also describes Petit still working the vineyards and orchards with a few helpers, keeping his involvement rooted in growing as well as ownership.
identity_note: The producer’s technical sheet confirms Clos Beylesse in 150 cl format. Vintage is unknown. Petit is documented as the historical grower-owner; the supplied research does not establish him as the current winemaker.

title: Two Years Before Separation
anecdote:
Gérard Bertrand bought the estate in 2016 and singled out an enclosed vineyard within the larger property for his rosé project. His team first vinified the broader vineyard for two years; observations of the selected parcels then led him to have them vinified separately for Clos du Temple.

By his June 2019 interview, a cellar dedicated to the clos was under construction. Bertrand described the project as a continuation and further development of his earlier rosé work at La Sauvageonne: a new cuvée taking shape through parcel selection, separate vinification and dedicated infrastructure.
identity_note: Exact cuvée matched; AOP Languedoc Cabrières. Vintage unknown: this is the cuvée’s origin story, not an account of a catalog vintage. The producer also lists Mourvèdre and Viognier; the catalog blend is incomplete and does not establish vintage-specific composition. Bertrand is documented as purchaser and creator, not sole cellar winemaker.

title: A Commandaria of His Own
anecdote:
Costas Tsiakkas decided to make his own Commandaria after attempts to change production through his village cooperative bank failed. A 2004 article about Tokaji’s renewal had helped prompt his rethink, but securing grapes meant persuading growers worried about their contracts with larger wineries.

He rented cooperative space, bought a mobile cooling unit and two steel tanks, and committed to buying one grower’s entire crop from two vineyards. In the 2023 interview, he reported still working with that grower. He also stopped fortifying his Commandaria in 2008.
identity_note: The catalog vintage is unknown. This history concerns Costas’s development of Tsiakkas Commandaria, not sole authorship or production specifications for the unidentified release.

title: From Cave to Family Garage
anecdote:
Benjamín Romeo bought a centuries-old cave beneath the castle of San Vicente de la Sonsierra in 1995. He made small batches there while acquiring vineyards, and produced Contador’s first vintage in 1999. The cave was the starting point for a venture that soon needed more room.

After favorable reception from buyers and the specialist press, Romeo committed himself full-time to his own project in 2000. The following year, he converted and equipped his parents’ garage in San Vicente for winemaking, giving the operation greater vinification capacity than the cave could accommodate.
identity_note: The catalog identifies Contador, not the separate La Cueva del Contador. No vintage is supplied; this history does not establish where the catalog wine was made.

title: Rebuilding Corton with Chardonnay
anecdote:
The Latour family replanted its Corton vineyards with Chardonnay after phylloxera devastated the vines in the late nineteenth century. Rather than simply restoring what had grown there before, the family changed the grape—a decision Maison Louis Latour explicitly connects to the creation of its Corton-Charlemagne.

The rebuilding also involved grafting vines onto resistant North American rootstocks, according to the producer’s history. Choosing Chardonnay was therefore part of a broader response to the vineyard’s destruction: the family changed both what it planted on Corton and how its damaged vineyards were replanted.
identity_note: Vintage unknown; the 2001 archive confirms the cuvée, not this bottle’s year. Producer accounts differ on the individual replanter’s identity and the previous grape varieties, so attribution remains with the Latour family.

title: Two Different Paths to Succession
anecdote:
Marcel Guigal took over the family house in 1961 after his father, Étienne, suffered total blindness, described in the estate’s history as temporary. His wife, Bernadette, joined him in 1973, and together they worked to expand the business behind wines including La Mouline.

Their son Philippe’s arrival followed a longer preparation: he spent nearly five years assisting Marcel with technical work before officially joining as winemaker in 1997. He made his first vintage that year, bringing a third generation into the Guigal cellar after an apprenticeship alongside his father.
identity_note: Exact producer and cuvée match confirmed. This is a producer-level succession story, not a documented La Mouline-specific decision. No vintage is supplied, so this bottle cannot be attributed to either generation’s vintage.

title: Reviving a Father's Memory
anecdote:
Marcel Guigal chose to revive La Turque after nearly fifty years without wine production at the site. The family replanted it in 1980 and 1981, drawing on his father Étienne’s memories of its wines from his years at Vidal-Fleury, before he founded Maison Guigal.

The revival yielded Guigal’s first La Turque vintage in 1985, under Marcel’s direction. His son Philippe later credited Marcel with the decision to bring the vineyard back; Philippe officially joined as winemaker in 1997, so the inaugural wine belongs to an earlier chapter of the family’s work.
identity_note: The catalog identifies E. Guigal’s La Turque but supplies no vintage. The 1985 date concerns the cuvée’s inaugural Guigal vintage, not this bottle.

title: Seventeen Parcels, Studied Separately
anecdote:
Stéphane Ogier joined his family’s estate in 1997 and chose to vinify its vineyard sites separately, a direction the domaine links to his experience in Burgundy. He later succeeded his father Michel, keeping individual parcels at the heart of his work.

In a January 2015 interview, Ogier described roughly fifteen years spent studying the individual expression of 17 Côte-Rôtie parcels. That knowledge informed vineyard work, winemaking and maturation, then led him to classify his sites and reorganize where their wines belonged within the estate’s range.

title: Restoring Cabernet Franc
anecdote:
Alexandre de Malet Roquefort began restoring Cabernet Franc at Château La Gaffelière in 2001, reversing an earlier planting choice. After the 1956 frost destroyed many vines, his father had replanted with Merlot. Alexandre considered Cabernet Franc well suited to the estate’s clay and limestone and chose to give it more room.

The replanting programme brought the estate vineyard to approximately 40% Cabernet Franc, according to his interview. Dame de Gaffelière’s official page also identifies Merlot and Cabernet Franc, alongside selected foot-of-slope parcels and a dedicated vat room and cellar.

title: Choosing California Over Bordeaux
anecdote:
Darioush Khaledi considered establishing a winery on Bordeaux’s Right Bank, but chose California for greater freedom in winemaking. His love of Bordeaux wines helped inspire Darioush; rather than settle there, the founder and his wife, Shahpar, built their winery around southern Napa and mountain sites.

That choice took shape through owning and farming vineyards, with an emphasis on cooler, less expected corners of Napa Valley. The connection to Darius II is documented: its 2014 release named the estate’s Apadana Block among its sources, alongside Sage Vineyard and Pritchard Hill.
identity_note: Vintage unspecified; the 2014 sources do not establish this release’s vineyards. The catalog classifies the wine as a Bordeaux-Style Red Blend, while Darioush identifies Darius II as Cabernet Sauvignon. This bottle’s composition and winemaker are not established.

title: A Family House Reunited
anecdote:
Marie-Louise de Nonancourt revived Delamotte at Le Mesnil-sur-Oger in 1927. Her son Charles later led the house from 1948 to 1988. His brother Bernard learned the business alongside him at Delamotte before taking charge of Laurent-Perrier in 1949, another house their mother had purchased.

In 1988, Bernard brought Delamotte into the Laurent-Perrier group and acquired neighboring Salon, pairing Delamotte and Salon as sister houses. The house where he had learned alongside Charles thus became part of the group he led: a family apprenticeship followed, decades later, by a corporate reunion.
identity_note: The catalog identifies Delamotte Blanc de Blancs but establishes no vintage or release lot. This producer-level history does not identify the cuvée’s creator or the maker of this release.

title: Thirteen Harvests Before the Handover
anecdote:
Vincent Chaperon worked alongside Richard Geoffroy at Dom Pérignon for thirteen harvests before succeeding him as chef de cave on January 1, 2019. Their collaboration began in 2005, giving the handover a long shared history in the cellar rather than marking Chaperon’s arrival at the house.

Together they declared four vintages: 2005, 2006, 2009 and then 2008, in that order. The house’s June 2018 announcement linked the succession to Dom Pérignon Vintage 2008, calling that release the culmination of their collaboration. Chaperon’s new responsibilities covered existing vintages as well as future production.
identity_note: Producer-level story only: the catalog identifies no cuvée, vintage or release. Dom Pérignon makes vintage-only Champagne; the missing year means vintage unknown, not non-vintage. This bottle cannot be identified as 2008 or attributed solely to Chaperon.

title: Cork Returns to the Cellar
anecdote:
Frédéric Panaïotis and his cellar team chose to bring cork ageing back to Dom Ruinart Blanc de Blancs for the 2010 vintage, replacing metal crown caps. Panaïotis served as Ruinart’s cellar master from 2007 until his death in 2025; the house credits this decision to him and his team.

That choice also brought back manual disgorgement. Ruinart’s technical record for the 2010 lists both ageing under cork and disgorgement by hand, documenting how the team’s decision changed the cellar work used to make that particular release.
identity_note: The catalog identifies Dom Ruinart Blanc de Blancs, not Ruinart Blanc de Blancs, but supplies no vintage. title: Returning to Rebuild in Lingey
anecdote:
Davy Dosnon returned to his home village of Lingey after studying viticulture and working in Burgundy wine houses, with the aim of reassembling his family’s vineyards. The importer identifies him as both proprietor and winemaker, and records that return in its technical sheet for Récolte Brute.

That sheet describes an estate of 7.5 hectares under his care: two hectares owned, with the rest leased. It also records a specific cellar choice for Récolte Brute: fermentation in previously used Puligny-Montrachet barrels, placing a documented Burgundy connection alongside the rebuilding of his family holdings.

title: A Cabernet Newcomer Gets the Job
anecdote:
Fred Schrader recruited Thomas Rivers Brown in 2000, before Brown had made his first Cabernet Sauvignon. According to Double Diamond’s account, they met while Brown was working at a local wine shop; he had begun his Napa Valley winemaking career at Turley Cellars.

That appointment connects directly to this cuvée’s maker: Schrader names Brown as winemaker for Double Diamond Oakville Cabernet Sauvignon. Double Diamond also credits him with overseeing its viticulture and winemaking, extending his responsibility beyond the cellar to the vineyard.

title: The Return to Dão
anecdote:
João Cabral Almeida sought out winemakers he admired, working first with João Brito e Cunha and then with Anselmo Mendes. He later named Mendes as one of the strongest influences on his professional development outside his family, before returning to Dão, where he had lived until age 17.

Back in Dão, Almeida developed his Musgo and Líquen projects while teaching viticulture and practical cellar coursework at the Escola Superior Agrária de Viseu. In January 2020, he announced their forthcoming release as the first results of several years spent searching in the region.
identity_note: Producer-level story only: the catalog omits a cuvée name, and both Musgo and Líquen Encruzado are listed. Neither is conclusively identified. Vintage is unknown.

title: Eighteen Presses, One Short Window
anecdote:
Olivier and Enzo Fayard analyzed grapes with Château Sainte Marguerite’s vineyard and cellar teams before setting the 2025 harvest in motion. The brothers faced a compressed picking window: after a rainy spring and sunny summer, the estate reported that ripening had accelerated.

Picking began on the night of August 18 with coastal Rolle parcels, then expanded to Grenache and Cinsault. The estate coordinated 18 pneumatic presses alongside night harvesting to handle the closely timed parcels—a response to the season’s concentrated demands across the estate.
identity_note: Producer-level harvest story, not a documented Fantastique lot. The catalog vintage is unknown. Its Grenache/Cinsault/Syrah listing differs from the official 2025 Grenache/Cinsault/Rolle blend; neither establishes this release’s composition.

title: The Cellar Behind Brick Walls
anecdote:
Giulio Ferrari had his city-centre winery sealed behind brick walls before leaving Trento when it was bombed in 1943. The founder of Ferrari Trento took refuge in his native village, leaving the stored sparkling wines behind the masonry.

On his return, Ferrari found the wines intact, according to the house’s own history. Its account credits those surviving bottles with the emergence of its first reserve wines, recording the outcome under its 1945 milestone: a cellar-protection decision that became part of the producer’s reserve-wine history.
identity_note: Producer-level account: the protected bottles are not identified as Ferrari Brut. The catalog supplies no vintage; the matched Ferrari Brut cuvée is documented as non-vintage. The wartime story is the house’s retrospective account.

title: The Bottles Mauro Held Back
anecdote:
Mauro Lunelli concealed 5,000 bottles made from Maso Pianizza grapes in 1972, according to Ferrari’s history. Instead of releasing the batch immediately, the Ferrari winemaker kept it in the cellar. Those bottles emerged in 1980 as the first Giulio Ferrari Riserva del Fondatore—a different cuvée from this Rosé.

That decision belongs to a long chapter in Ferrari’s winemaking history. In its 2019 account, the house described Mauro as its head winemaker for almost forty years and named Ruben Larentis, who joined Ferrari in 1986, as his successor.
identity_note: The strongest match is Classic Line Ferrari Rosé Trentodoc Brut, but the catalog does not confirm the tier. Vintage is unspecified. This producer-level story concerns Giulio Ferrari Riserva del Fondatore, not the Rosé; the cataloged bottle’s winemaker is not established.

title: Learning, Then Breaking the Model
anecdote:
Giovanni Manetti learned from Franco Bernabei while working alongside his brother Marco in the 1970s. Recalling Flaccianello’s beginnings in a 2020 interview, Fontodi’s proprietor credited the wine’s oenologist as his mentor. He described their formative years as shaped by a production culture focused on volume and lower costs—a model they wanted to break.

Manetti dated Flaccianello’s debut to 1981, placing it within that deliberate departure. His account aligned their approach with working exclusively with Sangiovese rather than adding international varieties; Fontodi’s official cuvée page confirms Flaccianello’s Sangiovese identity.

title: Fresnet’s Glassware Experiment
anecdote:
Laurent Fresnet brought neuroscientist Gabriel Lepousez and designer Octave de Gaulle together to explore how presentation could change the experience of Mumm’s wines. Appointed Mumm’s cellar master in January 2020, he described the cuvées to Lepousez, then commissioned de Gaulle to turn those ideas into glassware.

The collaboration produced two contrasting glasses: one heavy, smooth and deep purple; the other lighter, externally frosted and textured. For a tasting in Reims, Fresnet selected three Mumm cuvées, including Grand Cordon Rosé, which was served in both a standard glass and the heavier purple one.

title: Guest Rooms Kept Wine Flowing
anecdote:
Adobe Guadalupe paired its wine operation with a bed-and-breakfast when visitors to the valley’s wineries had few places to stay. Proprietor Tru Miller later credited that choice with keeping the venture afloat: in a 2015 interview, she said the estate would have gone bankrupt without the guest rooms.

Miller also described head winemaker Daniel Lonnberg’s arrival as an important addition to the team carrying the estate forward after her husband’s death. Her account links the practical work of hosting visitors with the people who sustained Adobe Guadalupe’s wine operation.

title: Choosing the Barrel for Garrus
anecdote:
Bertrand Léon and the Château d’Esclans team chose large-format demi-muids for Garrus. In a June 2026 interview, the estate’s technical director explained the aim: to allow oak influence without letting wood dominate. The choice involved not just barrel size, but a balance of new and older vessels.

The estate’s 2024 Garrus sheet records that approach in practice: fermentation in new and second-year demi-muids, with temperature controlled individually for each barrel. That documented combination gives a concrete counterpart to Bertrand’s explanation of how the team approaches oak for this cuvée.

title: From Growers to Their Own Champagne
anecdote:
Gaston Chiquet and his brother Fernand chose in 1919 to keep their grapes, make Champagne and sell the finished wine themselves. Both working winemakers, they established Chiquet Brothers, joining the early growers who took production and sales into their own hands.

In 1935, Gaston separated from Fernand and established his own brand, the producer behind this Rosé Premier Cru. At the beginning of the 1950s, he and his son Claude expanded the family estate into Aÿ and Hautvillers, adding vineyard holdings that the estate says gave them more blending possibilities.
identity_note: The producer lists this cuvée as non-vintage. The catalog identifies no particular release, base year or disgorgement; the history does not link the vineyard expansion specifically to the rosé.

title: Fifty Variations of a Bottle
anecdote:
Villa Sparina’s Moccagatta family commissioned designer Giacomo Bersanetti to create the estate’s distinctive bottle. His starting point was an ancient amphora found during excavation work while the property was being restored: a discovery that became the basis for a new design.

Stefano Moccagatta, who leads the estate alongside siblings Massimo and Tiziana, says development took a year and a half and at least fifty variations. The family tested neck width, neck length, height and proportions before choosing the bottle adopted for their wines—an approach he credits to their parents.
identity_note: The producer is verified; the catalog most plausibly identifies the classic Gavi, but the tier is not conclusive. This bottle-design story concerns the producer, not an exclusive cuvée feature. Vintage is unspecified.
