title: A Partnership from Vineyard to Cellar
anecdote:
Grégory Patriat took on Jean-Claude Boisset’s combined vineyard-and-cellar role in 2002, after working at Château de Chorey-lès-Beaune and Domaine Leroy. He selects grapes and works with supplying growers willing to meet his requirements, linking the maison’s sourcing decisions with its winemaking.

Laure Guilloteau joined him in 2010, after a year representing the company’s wines in the United States. Their division of labor gives Patriat the vineyards and broker relationships, while Guilloteau handles commercial contacts and stock management. They come together again for harvest and vinification across the house’s wines.
identity_note: The catalog matches the unqualified Gevrey-Chambertin, not a named-site bottling. Vintage unknown. The partnership is documented at producer level, not specifically for this cuvée.

title: From Finance to Vineyard Change
anecdote:
Romain Taupenot returned to manage his family’s domaine in 1998 after business studies in Paris and a career in finance. The importer documents him running Taupenot-Merme alongside his sister Virginie: a return to a family business where he had helped with harvest as a child.

In 2001, the domaine moved to organic farming. Looking back in a 2015 interview, Romain distinguished that change from his father’s earlier lutte raisonnée approach. The documented shift was in how the estate managed its vineyards, rather than a claim about how its wines tasted.
identity_note: The catalog identifies the village-level Gevrey-Chambertin, not Premier Cru Bel Air. Vintage is unknown; this producer-wide story does not establish the farming practices or maker of the particular release.

title: Leaving to Learn, Returning to Terrazas
anecdote:
Gonzalo Carrasco joined Terrazas de los Andes for a short stint in 2002, then left to work harvests elsewhere. He kept an ambition to return as a winemaker or technician, choosing practical experience away from the estate before finding his way back.

His overseas work took him to wineries in Australia, Spain and France. A later interview caught him approaching ten years back at Terrazas; in August 2020, he was documented as its senior winemaker. The departure had become a sustained return to the estate where he had started.
identity_note: Grand Malbec is verified, but the catalog gives no vintage. This is a producer-level historical story, not evidence that Carrasco created this cuvée or made the unidentified bottle. title: A Different Bargain with Growers
anecdote:
IXSIR replaced payment by the kilogram with long-term leases covering whole vineyards. In a 2020 interview, co-founder Gabriel “Gabi” Rivero, then chief winemaker and technical manager, described this change in the producer’s dealings with its grape growers: the arrangement resembled French fermage rather than buying grapes by weight.

Rivero credited the farmers with already knowing viticulture and delivering grapes in good condition. Under IXSIR’s approach, he reported, the team reduced yields while growers earned more money. The change paired vineyard management with better compensation for the people tending the vines.

title: An Opportunity in Noble Rot
anecdote:
Tonino Guzzo, Gorghi Tondi’s consulting enologist from its beginnings, recognized noble rot on Grillo grapes left on the vines into late October. He had encountered it before in another Sicilian vineyard and proposed to Michele Sala that they vinify the fruit rather than dismiss it as damaged.

That decision led to Grillodoro, first produced in 2006, with selective harvesting that requires repeated passes, sometimes for just a few bunches or individual berries. This is a separate Grillo wine from Kheirè, but its origins document an experiment by the same estate and its consultant.
identity_note: The catalog identifies Kheirè Grillo Riserva but supplies no vintage; the 2022 technical sheet does not establish the bottle’s year. This producer-level story concerns Grillodoro, not Kheirè, and does not imply that Kheirè uses botrytized grapes or was devised by Guzzo.

title: Cooling Grapes, Keeping Gravity
anecdote:
Marion and Manfred Ebner-Ebenauer built a dedicated grape-cooling facility at their estate in Poysdorf, aiming to prevent aroma loss and preserve their house style. Adding refrigeration did not mean replacing their gravity-led cellar workflow: juice still moves without pumps.

That cellar decision sits alongside a harvest practice used for every estate wine: hand-picking into 25-kilogram crates, intended to avoid damaging grape skins. Manfred is responsible for the cellar work, linking the new cooling facility with the retained pump-free processing rather than a wholesale change in how the estate handles its grapes.
identity_note: The producer and grape match, but the abbreviated catalog name identifies no specific Grüner Veltliner bottling or vintage. This producer-level account does not establish whether the unknown harvest preceded the undated cooling installation.

title: Two Parcels, Then Haiku
anecdote:
Castello di Ama chose to try Cabernet Franc when planting the second section of its Montebuoni vineyard, completed in 2001. After studying the soil and climate, the team introduced a variety not previously used at Ama, setting aside about two hectares in land-register parcels 84 and 85.

The estate’s account links that vineyard experiment to Haiku, whose first vintage arrived in 2009, combining Cabernet Franc with Sangiovese and Merlot. The trial and debut both fell within Marco Pallanti’s tenure: he had arrived in 1982 as a young agronomist taking charge of winemaking.

title: Years of Rosé Trials
anecdote:
Henriot spent several years testing a rosé before adding it to the house collection in the early 1980s, during the Henriot family’s seventh generation. The team’s challenge was to create a rosé that kept blending at the heart of the wine, rather than departing from the house’s approach.

The resulting cuvée brings together wines from multiple years and incorporates still red wine made from grapes grown in a particular parcel in Aÿ. That parcel is a concrete part of the rosé’s construction, alongside the multi-year blending the team chose to preserve.

title: From Orchard to Vineyard
anecdote:
Stephen and Prue Henschke bought a 13-hectare orchard at Lenswood in 1981, planning to turn it into vineyard using lessons from their time at Geisenheim in Germany. Prue initially kept the orchard running; Henschke intended research there to inform its older Barossa and Eden Valley vineyards too.

The 1983 Ash Wednesday bushfires destroyed the fruit trees. After the blackened stumps were removed, the property was planted to five wine-grape varieties. From the late 1980s, Prue spent years trialling clones to find which performed best at Lenswood.
identity_note: Producer-level story: no source connects Lenswood fruit or specific research outcomes to Henry’s Seven. The cuvée is verified, but its vintage is unknown.

title: Replanting the Family Hillside
anecdote:
Jean-Louis Chave began replanting Bachasson in Saint-Joseph in 1995, returning to a hillside his ancestors had worked for centuries. The family had abandoned it after phylloxera around 1880, leaving the ground without vines for more than a century before his restoration began.

The final vines were replanted in 2007. In a November 2023 interview, Chave singled out restoring Saint-Joseph vineyards, especially Bachasson, as his greatest source of pride: a project stretching across twelve years, on land tied to his family long before he began his own vineyard work in 1992–1993.
identity_note: Probable Domaine Jean-Louis Chave Hermitage Rouge, but the catalog does not distinguish it conclusively from Farconnet or Cuvée Cathelin. Vintage unspecified. This producer-level story concerns Bachasson in Saint-Joseph, not the source of Hermitage grapes.

title: From Architecture to the Cellar
anecdote:
Barbara Widmer joined her first Brancaia harvest in 1993 while studying architecture. The experience turned her toward winemaking. In 1994, she undertook a year-long internship at Domaine des Balisiers, an organic producer in Geneva, then began studying oenology at Wädenswil in 1995.

She returned to Brancaia as a qualified oenologist in 1998, the year its own cellar in Radda was completed. That cellar allowed the estate to vinify and mature its wines independently for the first time: a practical change accompanying her arrival in the family business.
identity_note: IL BLU is verified as Brancaia’s IGT Rosso Toscana. Vintage unknown; this is a producer-level story, not attribution of a particular release. IL BLU was first produced in 1988, before Barbara’s first harvest; she is not credited as its creator.

title: Sixty-Three Parts Before the Blend
anecdote:
Pierre Seillan divided Tenuta di Arceno’s vineyards into smaller units according to their soils, rather than treating each vineyard uniformly. During replanting, the estate mapped soil, topography and climate, creating a plan of 63 micro-crus. Seillan, the founding winemaker, leads this approach with resident winemaker Lawrence Cronin.

Each micro-cru is farmed, harvested and vinified separately, keeping its wine distinct until the final production stages. Il Fauno’s 2020 technical sheet names Arceno di Sotto, La Curva, Colombaio and San Giovanni as principal source blocks, connecting the cuvée to the team’s parcel-by-parcel work.

title: From Architecture to Ilatraia
anecdote:
Barbara Widmer turned from architecture toward wine after her first Brancaia harvest in 1993. She tested that choice with a year-long internship at Domaine des Balisiers in Geneva in 1994, then began studying oenology at Wädenswil in 1995.

She returned as a qualified oenologist in 1998, when Brancaia’s new Radda cellar first allowed independent vinification and maturation. That year, Bruno and Brigitte Widmer also bought the Maremma property and planted its first vineyards. A small harvest followed in 2000; those vineyards became the source of Ilatraia, first made in 2002.
identity_note: The catalog gives no vintage. Ilatraia’s constituent varieties have changed over time, so the listed grapes do not establish a vintage-specific blend. Sources do not attribute the Maremma purchase or original cuvée solely to Barbara.

title: When Imperial Was Withheld
anecdote:
CVNE withheld Imperial in 2002, 2003, 2006 and 2013 because those harvests did not meet its requirements. Grapes intended for Imperial went into other CVNE wines instead: selection could mean making no Imperial at all, rather than releasing it every year.

During the unfinished 2020 harvest, María Larrea assessed incoming fruit from vineyards supplying Imperial Reserva and Gran Reserva. She was optimistic about its prospects, but the decision remained open. Months of tastings and analytical checks still lay ahead before the wines entered their final aging stages.
identity_note: Vintage unknown. These are documented Imperial producer-level decisions, not events tied to this bottle; the historical non-release decisions are not attributed personally to Larrea.

title: One Brunello Instead of Three
anecdote:
Casanova di Neri chose to make just one Brunello in 2014, after a season of cold, rain and humidity that improved only toward late September. For the first time, the estate combined grapes intended for Tenuta Nuova, Cerretalto and Etichetta Bianca rather than releasing its separate Brunello selections.

The decision came during Giacomo Neri and his son Giovanni’s shared responsibility for viticulture and winemaking. Giacomo had taken over the estate in 1991; Giovanni joined in 2012. Their work also connects to Irrosso: the younger Giovanni is credited with notes on its official technical sheets.
identity_note: Producer-level story, not an Irrosso production change. Official identity: Irrosso Toscana IGT, Sangiovese with other varieties, not varietal Sangiovese. Vintage unspecified; the 2022 sheet does not identify this catalog wine’s vintage. The retailer’s conflicting Sant’Antimo Rosso DOC designation does not override the producer.

sources.title: Casanova di Neri - Azienda Agricola Vini
Casanova di Neri - Azienda Agricola La Storia

title: Blending for the Season
anecdote:
Scott Shirley, JUSTIN’s winemaker, weighed a cooler, wetter growing season when shaping the 2019 ISOSCELES. In the estate’s Spring 2022 newsletter, he described how those conditions prompted careful deliberation over which grape varieties should go into that year’s blend.

The selection also reached down to individual vineyard blocks. Rather than follow a fixed recipe, the team assembled the 2019 cuvée from varieties and blocks chosen to suit that season—a documented example of how the makers approached ISOSCELES, with the growing year guiding the final blend.
identity_note: The catalog vintage is unknown. This account concerns the documented 2019 ISOSCELES, not necessarily the catalog bottle. The producer newsletter’s indexed text was available, but the PDF returned an error when opened directly.

title: Beyond Payment by Weight
anecdote:
Gabriel “Gabi” Rivero described IXSIR’s shift away from paying growers by grape weight in a 2020 interview. The co-founder and chief winemaker explained that long-term arrangements covered entire vineyards instead. He reported that IXSIR reduced yields while growers earned more, changing the link between vineyard work and payment.

IXSIR’s 2020 press kit adds the practical framework: long-term grape-purchase contracts, technical assistance and strict quality controls. The estate reported that this approach helped more than 250 local farming families remain on their land—a producer-reported outcome of its grower relationships.
identity_note: The catalog’s Grand Reserve matches IXSIR Grande Réserve Red. Vintage is unspecified. This producer-level story does not identify which growers supplied this bottle.

sources.title: Ixsir: the new star on the Lebanese wine scene – wineanorak.com

title: A Cellar Built to Fit
anecdote:
Angéline Templier-Lassalle ordered fermentation tanks with lower doors and locking mechanisms that required less force when she returned to Champagne J. Lassalle. The founder’s granddaughter joined as winemaker in 2006. In a 2014 interview, she described a regular team of just four, with substantial cellar work falling to her personally.

These practical changes coexisted with older equipment: the house was still using its 1956 grape press. Angéline described her aim as maintaining traditional Champagne-making, adapting the working arrangements without replacing the inherited production system wholesale.
identity_note: The catalog matches J. Lassalle Brut Cuvée Préférence Premier Cru. Vintage and release are unknown. This is a producer-level story; the sources do not link the tank changes to Préférence specifically.

sources.title: Brut “Cuvée Préférence” 1er Cru | Champagne J. Lassalle | Kermit Lynch Wine Merchant

title: Restoring Kalmoesfontein’s Working Cellar
anecdote:
Adi and Hein Badenhorst acquired Kalmoesfontein in 2008 and set about restoring a property that needed work. The cousins restored the old cellar and planted new vines, rebuilding the practical foundations of their family winery rather than taking over a ready-made operation.

Today, Adi’s back-to-basics approach guides the cellar team, which uses old cement fermentation vessels and basket presses. For Kalmoesfontein White Blend, the estate documents another practical choice: most selected vineyard parcels are whole-bunch pressed together, then transferred to old casks for co-fermentation.
identity_note: Vintage unknown: no year appears in the catalog name. The estate dates acquisition to 2008 and separately describes the cousins’ arrival in 2007.

sources.title: About AA Badenhorst Family Wines | Kalmoesfontein Swartland – A. A. Badenhorst Family Wines
Kalmoesfontein Wine Collection | AA Badenhorst Family Wines – A. A. Badenhorst Family Wines

title: Twelve Years, One Blend
anecdote:
Maison Krug’s cellar team built Grande Cuvée 170ème Édition around the uneven 2014 harvest, when alternating hot, dry spells and cool, rainy periods left considerable differences between plots. They selected individual plot wines from eleven additional years, bringing the blend to 195 wines from twelve years.

Cellar master Julie Cavil’s account identifies some of those choices: reserve Pinot Noir from Ambonnay’s 2005 harvest, Chardonnay from Avize and Mesnil-sur-Oger across several years, and reserve Meunier, notably from 2013. The oldest wines in the finished blend date to 1998.
identity_note: 170ème is an edition number, not a vintage. Cavil became cellar master in January 2020, succeeding Éric Lebel; her account does not establish sole authorship of this blend.

sources.title: Krug Grande Cuvée 170ème Édition | Champagne Krug

title: From Cellar Work to Harvest Decisions
anecdote:
Michel Fauconnet joined Laurent-Perrier in 1973, working through cellar jobs before becoming cellar master and production manager in 2004. His apprenticeship led to a precise responsibility for Cuvée Rosé: the house’s April 2024 account describes him monitoring ripeness in each selected vineyard and approving its picking date.

Laurent-Perrier also worked with growers to select vineyards for this cuvée and adapted selected estate parcels, using green harvesting when needed. After picking, the Pinot Noir was sorted and destemmed before entering dedicated maceration tanks—a documented sequence linking vineyard selection to cellar work.
identity_note: No bottle vintage is supplied; 1968 is the cuvée’s launch year. These practices are documented in 2024, not attributed to this particular bottle. Olivier Vigneron is recorded as cellar master in 2025; Fauconnet is not presented as the current incumbent.

sources.title: Cuvée Rosé, l’expression du Pinot Noir - Laurent-Perrier

title: From Cellar Work to La Cuvée
anecdote:
Michel Fauconnet joined Laurent-Perrier in 1973 and learned through successive jobs as cellar worker, supervisor and head of the cellar. In 2004, he became the house’s third cellar master and production manager, taking responsibility for supplies and oversight from vinification through bottling.

Laurent-Perrier launched La Cuvée in 2017, during Fauconnet’s tenure, describing it as the outcome of long-term work on the quality of its supply. That connects this brut to the sourcing and production chain he oversaw, without crediting him as its sole creator.
identity_note: La Cuvée is designated non-vintage; the catalog identifies no particular batch or disgorgement. Fauconnet held the role at launch; Olivier Vigneron succeeded him in 2025.

title: Horses Before Certification
anecdote:
Château Latour reintroduced horses for ploughing in 2008. The following year, its vineyard teams began reviewing their existing methods, progressively changing cultivation and vine protection. Staff gradually trained in the new practices, making the transition a change in everyday work as well as vineyard management.

By August 2015, the entire vineyard was managed organically; certification followed in August 2018, extending to the winery and vinification. Le Pauillac de Château Latour draws partly on young vines outside the central Enclos, connecting this cuvée’s vineyard sources to the estate-wide transformation.
identity_note: The catalog matches Le Pauillac de Château Latour, not the Grand Vin or Les Forts de Latour. Vintage unknown; organic certification cannot be attributed to this bottle. The documented changes are estate-wide, not attributed to a sole individual.

sources.title: Château Latour | 01.In the beginning - From generation to generation
Château Latour | 01.In the beginning - The land of Pauillac

title: Two Weeks Before the Heat
anecdote:
Ornellaia’s team harvested Merlot early and quickly in 2020, completing the work in just two weeks. Its Le Volte 2020 technical sheet records the weather behind that compressed window: after a prolonged hot, dry summer, late-August rain brought cooler conditions, with nighttime temperatures falling to 13°C.

The team finished picking Merlot just before a week-long heatwave reached 37°C. That return of heat then forced another adjustment: harvesting of later-ripening vines began as early as September 17. The documented achievement was timing—the Merlot harvest was complete before the heat returned.
identity_note: The cuvée and producer are confirmed, but the catalog gives no vintage. This is a documented 2020 producer story, not an account of the unidentified bottle. The picking decisions are attributed to the team, not to a named individual.

title: Sixty Lots, Shared Decisions
anecdote:
Bertrand Roux, Rieussec’s cellar master, and estate director Mathieu Crosnier led the assessment of approximately sixty lots for the 2024 vintage. Rain throughout harvest had left Roux concerned before vinification; blending began in mid-January, with each participant scoring the wines from one to five.

A score of one indicated Château Rieussec; three indicated Carmes de Rieussec. Collective blind tasting helped keep attachment to a lot’s production history from deciding its place. Two divisive lots, one Sauvignon and one Sémillon, remained under debate until late in the process.
identity_note: The producer calls the matched cuvée Carmes de Rieussec, without the catalog’s initial “Les”; it is Château Rieussec’s second wine. No catalog vintage is identified. The 2024 episode is producer-level background, and the source does not establish that the two debated lots entered Carmes.

sources.title: Blending notes - Domaines Barons de Rothschild (Lafite)

title: A Foothold in Dão
anecdote:
João Cabral de Almeida secured his first Dão winemaking space in 2018, after working in Vinho Verde and the Douro. By 2022, his small cellar was in Oliveira de Barreiros, Silgueiros, and his approach centered on selecting vineyard sites and buying grapes.

Rather than relying solely on estate vines, he built close relationships with growers and followed their parcels throughout the year. That work took shape in the Musgo and Líquen labels; by the 2022 report, his Dão project had reached approximately 25,000 bottles across the range.
identity_note: The catalog entry is undated; its vintage remains unknown. Source 0 identifies João as winemaker for the 2018 Líquen Alfrocheiro, but that vintage cannot be assigned to this entry. The bottle count concerns the Dão project, not this cuvée alone.

sources.title: Descoberta: O Dão de João Cabral de Almeida - Grandes Escolhas

title: Preserving Cristal’s Old Vines
anecdote:
Jean-Baptiste Lécaillon joined the Rouzaud family in a late-1990s review of Louis Roederer’s vineyards. Their questions moved from regenerating soils to preserving the diversity and longevity of planting material. For that work, the team selected healthy, promising vines from Domaine Cristal’s pre-clonal vineyards, planted before the 1960s.

In the early 2000s, cuttings from those selected Cristal vines were replanted in four propagation conservatories: two in Aÿ, one in Verzenay and one in the Côte des Blancs. The selections included both Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, preserving old-vine material for future planting.
identity_note: Provisionally matched to white Cristal; vintage unknown. The producer identifies Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, not the catalog’s Meunier. This vineyard-material story does not establish that the unidentified bottle contains grapes from the propagated selections.

sources.title: T H E E X P R E S S I O N O F

title: Vineyards Before the Blend
anecdote:
Jean-Claude Rouzaud selected Pinot Noir plots in Aÿ and Chardonnay plots in Avize and Le Mesnil-sur-Oger before making the first Cristal Rosé blend from the 1974 harvest. Then responsible for Louis Roederer’s vineyards and cellars, he built the new cuvée around those chosen sites.

His work also helped develop Roederer’s infusion method. For Cristal Rosé, Chardonnay juice is added to macerating Pinot Noir grapes, and the two ferment together: a documented production choice that connects the cuvée’s creation with the method the house describes today.
identity_note: Exact cuvée matched; vintage unspecified. Official documentation lists Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, not the catalog’s Meunier. Rouzaud was the creator, not the current cellar master; the story does not establish who supervised this particular bottle.

sources.title: Chapter 1 THE TURNING POINT IN 1974 A masterpiec

title: A Project Across Borders
anecdote:
Laila Maghathe established Love Letter in Lebanon in 2021 while also making wine in southern Australia. Her Lebanese project uses shared winery space at Mersel: the connection behind this catalog entry, rather than a claim that she makes Mersel’s entire range.

Living in Cincinnati, Maghathe travels annually to Lebanon between growing seasons. In her interview with Henna Bakshi, she describes weighing possible border closures and war before flying, yet choosing to continue making wine there. That recurring journey sustains her own project within the shared winery.
identity_note: The catalog’s Merlot matches Love Letter by Laila within the Mersel portfolio. Vintage remains unknown. Other Love Letter wines use different grapes; their details are not applied here.

CRITIC’S CORNER | Henna Bakshi - 67 Pall Mall

title: The Debut David Abreu Delayed
anecdote:
David Abreu made a few barrels of Cabernet from Madrona Ranch in 1986, then withheld them: he did not consider the wine good enough for his first release. The vineyard developer’s debut waited until 1987, the first Abreu wine he sold.

Abreu introduced that wine personally, leaving bottles with Napa Valley restaurants for staff to try and inviting them to contact him if interested. The estate later declassified Madrona Ranch’s 1988, 1990 and 1998 wines too; its history links his eventual acquisition of a winery to gaining greater control over execution.
identity_note: No catalog vintage is specified. The catalog classifies the wine as Cabernet Sauvignon; Abreu describes its single-site wines as Cabernet blends. David Abreu’s documented historical role does not establish who made the unidentified catalog vintage.

title: One Parcel, Its Own Wine
anecdote:
Donne Fittipaldi selected Cabernet Franc from the oldest parcel of its historic vineyard on Via Bolgherese to make Magnetic. The family had chosen to plant vineyards in Bolgheri in 2004; this separate cuvée drew on that planting history, with its fruit sourced from Vigna del Bruciato.

For Magnetic’s maturation, the estate team chose cocciopesto vessels, presenting the decision as a way to revisit the past through contemporary winemaking. The technical sheet records 2019 as the wine’s first production year: a documented milestone for the cuvée, rather than a date inferred from the catalog entry.
identity_note: Magnetic is identified by the estate as Bolgheri Rosso Magnetic. The catalog entry has no vintage; 2019 is the first production year, not this bottle’s established vintage. Parcel selection and vessel choice are credited collectively to the estate, not personally to oenologist Emiliano Falsini.

title: Two Generations, One Vineyard
anecdote:
Emilio Moro and his son, also named Emilio, planted Pago de Sanchomartín in 1964. The estate’s family history records the two generations working the vineyards together: their connection to the site behind this wine was the practical work of growing vines.

The younger Emilio went on to establish the commercial winery with his children in 1987. In 2002, the estate launched Malleolus de Sanchomartín, naming the cuvée for that vineyard—a documented link between the family’s planting work and a wine introduced nearly four decades later.
identity_note: Vintage unknown. The producer identifies Tempranillo; the catalog’s “(Blend)” classification is unsubstantiated. The wine page gives conflicting planting dates, 1944 and 1964; 1964 is supported by the separate estate history. The younger Emilio died in 2008 and is not presented as today’s winemaker.

sources.title: Vinos Emilio Moro | Bodegas Emilio Moro

title: A Third Wine, Deliberately Selected
anecdote:
Château Margaux chose to keep its third red wine in 2009 rather than sell it in bulk. The team matured it in barrel with the same care as Pavillon Rouge, then bottled it as Margaux du Château Margaux. In 2010, it added a fourth selection for less successful lots, still sold in bulk.

In 2013, late-ripening plots and uneven fruit development prompted another reshuffle. The team redirected selected Pavillon Rouge lots into Margaux du Château Margaux and downgraded nearly a quarter of production to the fourth selection. That year’s third wine consisted entirely of wines that previously would have entered Pavillon Rouge.
identity_note: This is Château Margaux’s third red wine, not its Grand Vin or Pavillon Rouge. The catalog supplies no vintage; the dated decisions describe the cuvée’s history, not this unidentified bottle. Sources credit the estate team collectively.

title: A Partnership Before the Blends
anecdote:
João Carlos Paes Mendonça invited Dirk Niepoort to develop Quinta Maria Izabel’s wine project with freedom to pursue his own approach. Before committing, Niepoort wanted Gabriela Canossa’s collaboration and a workable relationship with the owner. He travelled to Recife and spent several days with Paes Mendonça before the partnership took shape.

The estate’s early production divided responsibilities: Canossa was the resident winemaker, while Niepoort did not participate in the first harvest, in 2012, but took responsibility for the final red-wine blends. The estate’s official team page identifies his role as consulting oenologist.
identity_note: Maria Izabel Tinto is distinct from the Quinta Maria Izabel range. Vintage is unknown. This producer-level account does not establish who made the undated bottle or identify the early blends as this exact cuvée.

title: A Harvest Handover by Telephone
anecdote:
Ramzi Ghosn took charge of winemaking at Massaya midway through the 2004 harvest, after the estate dismissed its winemaker. It was his first time making the wines. Daniel and Frédéric Brunier helped him guide the fermentations through daily telephone calls, providing practical support while the harvest was already under way.

That collaboration continued without handing over final control. In November 2018, Massaya reported that its French partners helped assess 46 separate harvest batches, while Ramzi and his brother Sami retained the final winemaking decisions at the estate.
identity_note: Gold Reserve is verified as a Massaya wine, but its vintage is unknown. These accounts concern the producer; neither links the 2004 handover specifically to Gold Reserve nor identifies who made this bottle.

title: From Blend to Vineyard Bottling
anecdote:
Ted Edwards used Merlot from Stagecoach Vineyard’s M4 block in Freemark Abbey’s regular Merlot and Cabernet bottlings before he and his team considered giving it a separate bottling. For the 2014 vintage, Edwards and his assistant winemakers made a few hundred cases of Stagecoach Vineyard Merlot, alongside the existing Napa Valley Merlot.

That work included Gabrielle Shaffer, then Stagecoach’s viticulture and winery relations manager. She implemented Edwards’s specific requirements in the vineyard blocks, while he deferred to her knowledge of the vineyard’s soils and history: a collaboration linking cellar decisions with vineyard expertise.
identity_note: Producer-level story: the catalog establishes neither a vintage nor whether this is Napa Valley Merlot or the separate Stagecoach Vineyard Merlot. It does not verify M4 fruit or Edwards’s involvement in this bottle.

sources.title: Making a Statement with Stagecoach Merlot | Freemark Abbey

title: From Engineering to Winemaking
anecdote:
Ivo Jeramaz traded an engineering path for winemaking after coming to the United States in 1986 with help from his uncle, Miljenko “Mike” Grgich. Raised in a Croatian grape-growing family, he had helped make wine before earning a master’s degree in engineering at the University of Zagreb.

Drawn to Napa’s wine industry, Jeramaz apprenticed under Mike and added enology and viticulture classes at UC Davis to his practical training. He went on to become Grgich Hills Estate’s principal winemaker and vice president of vineyards and production.
identity_note: The catalog matches Grgich Hills Estate Napa Valley Merlot. Vintage is unknown; source 0 verifies the wine through a 2021 listing, not this bottle’s year. This producer-level story does not establish Jeramaz’s responsibility for the unidentified vintage.

title: Learning Beside Eddie
anecdote:
Eddie Chami works as Mersel’s winemaker, and his work became a route into wine for Abdullah Richi. After moving from Syria to Lebanon to escape the war, Abdullah became interested in winemaking and learned by observing Eddie—a documented connection within the producer behind LebNat.

Abdullah went on to develop Dar Richi Hanan, a still red named for his wife, first produced in 2018. In 2022 he followed it with Helem, a white wine. Establishing a winery in Syria remained an aspiration in Mersel’s account, rather than an accomplished next step.
identity_note: The catalog matches Mersel’s LebNat Pink Rosé. Vintage is unknown; 2019 is the cuvée’s launch year. Bekaa Valley is not verified as exclusive vineyard origin. This producer-level story does not establish that Abdullah worked on LebNat.

sources.title: . . . F O R T H E P E O P L E

title: Reclaimed Terraces, Early Bubbles
anecdote:
Nino Bevilacqua began buying abandoned, bramble-covered plots in 2008 to establish Terrazze dell’Etna. A Palermo engineer and the estate’s founding proprietor, he set a land-recovery project in motion. His family restored old vineyards, traditional palmenti wine-processing structures and stone terraces, which the estate says local workers cultivate by hand.

Sparkling wine was part of the founding project, not a later addition. The estate describes beginning with sparkling production as a deliberate challenge and identifies its first Nerello Mascalese vines as central to Rosé Brut, linking this cuvée to that early vineyard work.
identity_note: The catalog does not distinguish the standard Rosé Brut from the separate 50 mesi release; vintage is unknown. Bevilacqua is documented as founding proprietor, not as this release’s winemaker.

title: Renewing the Family Domaine
anecdote:
Xavier Monnot took over the family domaine in 1994 after completing his oenological studies. He began replanting parcels with both selections propagated from old vines and new clones, while also updating the cellar equipment—a renewal spanning vineyard and winery.

In 2005, after those changes, he began bottling under his own name. The property had previously been known as Domaine René Monnier, after his grandfather, who had begun some domaine bottling and acquired vineyard parcels with his wife. Le Limozin’s technical sheet records Xavier’s transition to his own label.
identity_note: Vintage unknown; the 2021 technical sheet confirms cuvée identity, not the catalog entry’s vintage. The renewal decisions are producer-level; Le Limozin is not documented as a replanted parcel.

sources.title: Xavier Monnot Meursault Le Limozin 2021 - Winebow

title: When Michel Opened the Cellar
anecdote:
Michel Mailliard tracked the maturation of cellar-held wines through tastings across different years. The house’s newsletter names Brut Grégory among the cuvées used for these comparisons: rather than releasing every bottle immediately, the team kept selected wines back and followed their development.

When Michel judged some of those retained wines ready, he chose to release limited quantities, creating the house’s Œnothèque range. Specially designed labels marked the releases, and the house announced plans to offer further cellar-held cuvées regularly—a new route from its reserves to release.
identity_note: Producer-level historical story; the unspecified bottle is not established as an Œnothèque release. Its vintage is unknown. The official Grégory listing names Chardonnay and Pinot Noir; the catalog’s Meunier attribution is unverified. Michel’s documented historical role does not establish him as the current winemaker.

title: A Newspaper Route to Ruffino
anecdote:
Gabriele Tacconi answered a newspaper advertisement for a Tuscan winemaking job while working on Sicily’s Mount Etna. That opportunity brought him to Ruffino in 1998. He had left home to study winemaking and viticulture in Milan before beginning his career in Sicily.

At Ruffino, his predecessor urged him to protect the established wines and house style, rather than make changes merely to leave his mark. By 2019, Tacconi was chief winemaker, overseeing a 12-person team and describing his role as collaborative rather than imposing a personal style.
identity_note: Modus is distinct from Modus Primo; vintage is unknown. This is a producer-level story, not attribution of this bottle to Tacconi. Modus debuted in 1997, before his 1998 arrival. The historical interviews do not establish his current role.

sources.title: Can Ruffino Winery Stay True to Its Roots?
John Schreiner on wine: Ruffino: an anchor name in Chianti

title: Rebalancing Brut Impérial
anecdote:
Benoît Gouez increased the use of reserve wines and extended cellar time as part of a gradual revision of Moët & Chandon’s Brut Impérial. The cellar master described these connected changes when asked about the cuvée’s dosage falling from 11 to 7 grams per litre.

He also pointed to riper harvested grapes: together, these factors meant less sugar was needed for the balance he sought. Moët & Chandon’s current Brut Impérial product sheet lists 7 grams per litre, documenting the outcome of that evolution rather than a change in sugar alone.
identity_note: The catalog identifies white Brut Impérial, listed by the producer as non-vintage. Its release, base harvest and disgorgement are unknown; neither the current dosage nor a particular stage of Gouez’s changes can be assigned to this bottle.

sources.title: Benoît Gouez of Moët on champagne, climate change and more | Tatler Asia

title: Moscato Before the Reds
anecdote:
Carlo, Bruno, Giorgio and Giovanna Rivetti launched Bricco Quaglia and Biancospino in 1977 as separate, vineyard-identified Moscatos. Taking over from their grower parents, Giuseppe “Pin” and Lidia, the siblings began with the local vineyards and indigenous grapes their family knew, with their parents’ support.

Bricco Quaglia was therefore part of La Spinetta’s original undertaking, not a later addition to a red-wine estate. The family credits the success of its Moscato business with enabling the move into reds, beginning with Barbera Cà di Pian.
identity_note: The catalog vintage is unknown; 1977 is the cuvée’s launch year. Historical single-cru positioning does not establish this bottle’s sourcing: the current producer page lists both Bricco Quaglia and vineyards in Mango.

title: Meunier on Their Terms
anecdote:
Jean-Marc Moussé chose to join Club Trésors de Champagne in 2005, with a family condition: their Spécial Club would be entirely Meunier. His son Cédric, who had joined the estate in 2003, acted as liaison with the Club; he later explicitly credited his father with the decision.

The first Club wine was accepted in 2005. Skurnik links it to Les Fortes Terres, which Jean-Marc had already bottled separately as a vintage prestige cuvée. The Club chapter thus continued an existing choice to give this vineyard its own wine.
identity_note: Wine-specific sources identify Les Fortes Terres as 100% Meunier, unlike the catalog blend. No vintage or Spécial Club status is established for this bottle. Cédric’s explicit attribution to Jean-Marc is preferred over Skurnik’s older attribution to Cédric.

title: A Rejection Becomes No Name
anecdote:
Borgogno’s estate team turned a disputed certification into No Name. In the producer’s telling, the story began in 2008: a wine submitted to the Barolo tasting commission was rejected, despite the team’s confidence in it. A second sample of the same wine was then approved.

Rather than set aside the first verdict, the team chose to release the wine associated with that rejection as No Name. Borgogno presents the decision as a response to the inconsistency it perceived in certification, giving this cuvée an identity rooted in a specific disagreement.
identity_note: The technical sheet identifies No Name as Langhe Nebbiolo DOC. Vintage unknown; 2008 dates the reported episode, not this catalog wine. The account is Borgogno’s own, and no individual decision-maker is identified.

title: Changing the Cellar Routine
anecdote:
Maison Louis Latour adapted its red-wine cellar work to warmer Burgundy vintages. Its 2018 House Journal describes a collaboration between winemaker Jean-Charles Thomas and successive technical directors Boris Champy and Christophe Deola: a team revising established practice rather than simply keeping the routine unchanged.

Thomas had joined the house in 1995 and became winemaker in 2005. The documented changes gave the house’s reds somewhat more extraction, longer vatting and fewer rackings—the transfers of wine between barrels. These were concrete adjustments to how the team handled its red wines.
identity_note: The catalog matches Maison Louis Latour’s village-appellation Nuits-Saint-Georges, not a named premier cru. Vintage is unknown. This producer-level account does not establish Thomas’s responsibility for this bottle or when these methods reached this cuvée.

title: A Yeast of Their Own
anecdote:
Emilio Rodríguez led Terras Gauda’s experimental-cellar work in a four-year collaboration with Spain’s CSIC to select a yeast from the estate’s own vineyards. The team narrowed four vineyard-derived candidates to one, linking the winery’s trials with work in CSIC laboratories.

The winery reported regular, progressive fermentation in a large-scale trial during the 2007 harvest. By May 2008, Terras Gauda and CSIC jointly held the yeast patent. The 2024 Terras Gauda technical sheet specifies fermentation with its own selected yeast, connecting this research story to a documented release of the wine.
identity_note: O Rosal is the subregion, not a separate cuvée. The catalog vintage is unknown; the 2024 sheet does not establish this bottle’s vintage or which yeast was used for it.

sources.title: Terras Gauda y el CSIC patentan la levadura de albariño | Galicia Digital

title: Staying With One Yeast
anecdote:
Michael Silacci, Opus One’s winemaker, asked research manager Alaina Velasquez to inoculate a clay amphora with an experimental yeast candidate called Monkee in 2023, the estate’s first year using amphorae. She selected and propagated a candidate from her small-scale fermentations before DNA testing had established its identity.

When the fermentation developed an unpleasant smell, Velasquez proposed adding another strain. Silacci asked her to add more of the selected yeast instead. She reports that fermentation finished without issue; later DNA analysis identified her selection as the only non-commercial strain among the Monkee candidates submitted.
identity_note: Vintage unknown. This producer-level experiment is not documented as entering the final Opus One blend. Silacci’s retirement was announced for after the 2026 harvest.

title: Two Muscats, Different Choices
anecdote:
Cecilia Diaz and Guillermo Campos Baeza generally keep La Mariota’s schist and limestone sites separate. For Orange Tacsum, they make an exception: the cuvée brings together both landscapes, with Muscat d’Alexandrie from Bac de las Coves in Tautavel and Muscat à Petits Grains from Vingrau.

During a merchant’s vineyard visit, Guillermo explained another choice behind this blend: picking the Petits Grains slightly underripe to restrain its aromatic contribution. The two Muscats therefore meet in Orange Tacsum after different harvesting decisions, rather than being treated alike simply because they share a grape-family name.
identity_note: Vintage unknown; the 2021 technical sheet confirms identity, not this bottle’s year. The harvesting account documents a reported practice, not its application to every vintage. Classified as Vin de France.

sources.title: Cecilia et Guillermo - La Mariota - Buveur de vin

title: A Chance for Merlot
anecdote:
Dave Phinney accepted Merlot from growers who were considering pulling out their vines as demand weakened around 2005. Already supplying him with Cabernet Sauvignon, they offered to wait for payment until he had sold the finished wine. That purchase became part of Papillon’s origin story.

Phinney recalls that the first Papillon was Merlot-led, but his goal was to include all five Bordeaux varieties. He says that commitment continued as the blend changed between vintages; Orin Swift’s current Papillon page also confirms the five-variety focus.
identity_note: The catalog identifies no vintage. Phinney dates the fruit-buying opportunity to around 2005; the estate timeline lists Papillon as a 2007 new release. Neither establishes this bottle’s vintage.

Barrel to Bottle Podcast Episode: Dave Phinney of Orin Swift

title: Bringing Podere Fortuna Back
anecdote:
Tenuta Cafaggiolo brought seven hectares of Podere Fortuna back within the estate while seeking a suitable place to grow Pinot Nero. The team chose the site for its cooler conditions and pronounced differences between day and night temperatures: a specific vineyard decision behind the estate’s Pinot Nero program.

That program now centers principally on Pinot Nero, with smaller quantities of Chardonnay and rosato. Within it, Cafaggiolo describes Pater Patriae as a selection from the estate’s finest vines, connecting this cuvée to the team’s broader focus on the grape.
identity_note: Matched to Pater Patriae, Tenuta Cafaggiolo, Toscana IGT Pinot Nero. Vintage unknown. Sources do not establish this cuvée’s precise parcels or that all its fruit comes from the seven hectares; no individual winemaker is identified.

title: Keeping Acidity in Cortalto
anecdote:
Enrico Cerulli Irelli explained a change in the family’s Cortalto Pecorino in September 2018: the team had initially allowed malolactic fermentation, then reconsidered. They decided acidity was central to their interpretation of Pecorino and stopped allowing that fermentation for this wine.

The account accompanied the 2016 Cortalto Pecorino, tying the decision to this cuvée rather than to a general estate practice. Tenuta Cerulli Spinozzi also identifies Cortalto as coming from a single vineyard in Canzano: a specific origin for the wine whose cellar approach the family had revised.
identity_note: Catalog vintage unknown. The 2018 account concerns the 2016 wine; it does not establish the first vintage without malolactic fermentation or continuity in later vintages. Enrico was the family proprietor and estate manager, not the identified technical winemaker; the estate separately names Paolo Ulpiani as enologist.

title: Four Magnums, a New Cuvée
anecdote:
André Baveret rediscovered four custom-made magnums painted by Émile Gallé in 1964. Perrier-Jouët’s history links that rediscovery to the birth of Belle Époque: an existing piece of the house’s artistic heritage became part of the story of a new cuvée.

Baveret was Perrier-Jouët’s cellar master from 1964 to 1993, and its archive credits him with creating Belle Époque as well as Belle Époque Rosé. The original Belle Époque Brut first appeared in 1964, with a bottle bearing Gallé’s Japanese-anemone design from 1902.
identity_note: The shortened catalog name does not conclusively distinguish Brut from other Belle Époque releases, so this account uses producer scope. Vintage is unknown; 1964 is the original cuvée’s origin date, not this bottle’s vintage. Baveret is its historical creator, not necessarily the maker of this bottle.

title: A Second Chardonnay Creation
anecdote:
Hervé Deschamps personally selected the Chardonnay wines for Perrier-Jouët Blanc de Blancs, having already created the separate Belle Epoque Blanc de Blancs. Launched in 2017, his second Blanc de Blancs project was the house’s first addition to its collection in twenty years.

Before retiring in October 2020, Deschamps worked alongside his successor, Séverine Frerson, blending wines from the 2019 harvest and tasting older cuvées in the house’s wine library. That hands-on handover concerned the house’s cellar work; the documented sessions were not specifically linked to this cuvée.
identity_note: The catalog identifies the classic Blanc de Blancs, not Belle Epoque Blanc de Blancs. Vintage is unknown; 2017 is the launch year. Deschamps created the cuvée, but the unidentified bottling cannot be attributed to either his or Frerson’s tenure.

title: A Handover at the Blending Table
anecdote:
Séverine Frerson worked alongside Perrier-Jouët cellar master Hervé Deschamps before succeeding him. Announced in September 2018, the planned handover included tasting rare wines from the house library and blending wines from the 2019 harvest together, giving the two cellar masters a period of collaboration before responsibility changed hands.

In October 2020, following Deschamps’s retirement, Frerson became the house’s eighth cellar master and its first woman in the role. Perrier-Jouët also documents her practice of selecting base wines without first checking their vineyard origin, keeping that information out of her initial assessment.
identity_note: Exact cuvée verified. Vintage unknown. This producer-level succession story does not establish who blended this bottle; the jointly blended 2019 wines are not identified as Blason Rosé components.

title: Blending Before the Handover
anecdote:
Séverine Frerson worked alongside Hervé Deschamps on blending wines from the 2019 harvest before succeeding him as Perrier-Jouët’s eighth cellar master in October 2020. Their transition also included tasting rare wines from the house’s library, giving the incoming cellar master time with both her predecessor and the wines in his care.

At the handover, Deschamps passed Frerson the historical cellar books containing earlier cellar masters’ notes and observations. Alongside their shared blending work, she inherited a written record of decisions made by the people who had held the role before her.
identity_note: Producer-level story: the joint 2019-harvest blending is not documented as Grand Brut. No vintage is supplied, so this bottle cannot be assigned to either cellar master.

title: A Return, Then a Departure
anecdote:
Rodolphe Péters joined the family estate in 2007 after twelve years working in wine- and Champagne-related companies. An œnologist-winemaker, he succeeded his father, François, in 2008 and focused his efforts on the estate’s winemaking facilities.

In 2009, the house released Rosé for Albane, expanding a repertoire previously devoted exclusively to Blancs de Blancs Champagnes. Cuvée de Réserve remains the estate’s flagship: exclusively Chardonnay, combining more than twenty harvest years. The succession story belongs to its producer; the documented new release was a different cuvée.
identity_note: The catalog matches Pierre Péters Cuvée de Réserve Blancs de Blancs. No vintage or disgorgement is identified. The sources do not document a corresponding change to Cuvée de Réserve or establish that the facilities work caused the rosé release.

title: Keeping the Parcels Apart
anecdote:
Elena Walch installed a new cellar system in 2015 to separate berries from stems in four successive stages. At the estate, the aim was to avoid tearing or crushing the berries during that operation, rather than handling the harvest as one undifferentiated batch.

Gravity then carried the grapes, parcel by parcel, into small tanks, keeping vineyard lots separate through that stage of production. Julia and Karoline Walch, the family’s fifth-generation managers, continue the estate’s emphasis on precisely identified vineyard sites and parcels.
identity_note: The catalog matches Elena Walch Pinot Grigio, Alto Adige DOC; vintage is unknown. This is an estate-level story: the sources do not establish that this Pinot Grigio uses the described system or identify who commissioned its installation.

title: Opening the Blending Bench
anecdote:
Alois Lageder’s team opened PORER’s blending process to others with a kit of three separate barrel samples. The estate links its experiments with immediate pressing, short skin contact and extended contact with grapes, skins and stems to its search for responses to climate change.

The “Blend your own PORER” kit let participants combine those components themselves, rather than encounter only the finished wine. In May 2020, Clemens Lageder explained the project in a report documenting that samples had been sent to journalists and wine specialists.
identity_note: Cuvée confirmed; vintage unknown. The estate’s 2021 listing says Alto Adige DOC, while the research reports Mitterberg IGT in importer documentation. Neither classification can be assigned to this bottle without a vintage or label image; no component-contact duration is assigned here.

sources.title: In cantina - Lageder, tre versioni di Pinot Grigio per sfidare il clima

title: Raising the Vineyard Guardians
anecdote:
Antiquum Farm decided in summer 2020 to breed two Maremma guardian dogs, Opal and Dewey. Owner and farmer Stephen Hagen’s account explains the practical need: livestock-managed vineyards depended on dogs to protect the animals. Four of the farm’s dogs had proved capable of guarding multiple species while also welcoming visitors.

Opal delivered twelve puppies shortly before the 2020 harvest. The farm reported sending bonded, imprinted puppies to other farms and ranches, while choosing four—Gus, Pink, André and Churro—to stay as its next generation of livestock protectors.
identity_note: Daisy is verified, but the catalog supplies no vintage. This producer-level story does not establish a connection between the 2020 breeding decision and this bottle. Stephen Hagen is documented as owner and farmer, not as its cellar winemaker.

title: A Lease Built on Farming
anecdote:
Josh Bergström approached David and Valerie Hill in 2008 about leasing their entire eight-acre Le Pré du Col planting. As Bergström moved from purchased fruit toward estate-farmed vineyards, his team offered a specific commitment: introduce biodynamic farming and vineyard stewardship. The Hills agreed, and the partnership began.

By Josh’s 2016 account, the partners had planted another eight acres, doubling the vineyard to 16 acres. That same account identifies Bergström’s Le Pré du Col single-vineyard bottling, connecting this wine to the site secured through that farming agreement.
identity_note: Vintage unknown. The Hills’ ownership and lease arrangement are documented historically in Josh Bergström’s 2016 account, not independently verified as current.

sources.title: A focus on Le Pré du Col | Bergström Wines

title: Letting Two Wines Emerge
anecdote:
Maggie Harrison chose not to fix Antica Terra’s wine identities before seeing the year’s wines, despite wondering how customers would understand the producer. In a 2020 interview, the winemaker and co-owner described keeping lots separate, numbering samples from every barrel and blending them blind.

The team assembled and dismantled trial blends over three days, working eight to eleven hours daily. Harrison explained that a natural division on the blending table led to two counterpart bottlings: Ceras and Botanica. Rather than assigning their identities beforehand, the team let the blends determine the wines.
identity_note: The official archive confirms Antica Terra Botanica Pinot Noir. No vintage is supplied; the story documents Harrison’s approach described in 2020, not production decisions for an identified vintage.

sources.title: Interview: Antica Terra Winemaker Maggie Harrison - COOL HUNTING®

title: A Friendship Back to Oregon
anecdote:
Katie Santora joined Chehalem in 2012 after a friendship helped bring her back to Oregon. She had met Wynne Peterson-Nedry at UC Davis in 2007; a year later, Wynne helped her secure a harvest job at REX HILL, her introduction to working in Oregon.

In 2011, Wynne—then Chehalem’s head winemaker—reconnected with Santora in Salt Lake City and encouraged her to apply. After another harvest in Chile and an extensive hiring process, Santora joined as assistant winemaker. She planned to stay four years, but became head winemaker and led her first Chehalem harvest in 2018.
identity_note: Chehalem is a strong producer match, but the catalog identifies neither cuvée nor vintage. This is producer history; Santora’s responsibility for this bottle and its vineyard sources cannot be established.

sources.title: Winemaker Katie Santora Celebrates Ten Years At Chehalem - Chehalem Winery

title: A Field and a Winemaker
anecdote:
Robert Drouhin bought an undeveloped Dundee Hills property in 1987, established Domaine Drouhin Oregon and appointed his daughter Véronique as winemaker at the outset. She had first visited Oregon the year before; the purchase gave her a winemaking role at the new estate.

Véronique’s Oregon winemaking work began in 1988, and her responsibility has continued beyond that founding appointment: the estate says she still makes every Domaine Drouhin Oregon wine. In the cellar, she also selects barrels for the estate’s Pinot Noir cuvées before blending.
identity_note: The catalog identifies Domaine Drouhin Oregon but not a specific Pinot Noir cuvée. Vintage is unspecified; this story is producer-level.

title: Animals Among the Vines
anecdote:
Hanzell began implementing integrated farming in 2016, during Jason Jardine’s tenure as president and director of winemaking. The following year, chickens, sheep and pigs joined the estate, alongside two Maremma livestock guardian dogs, Scout and Radley.

In Jardine’s account, livestock rotate through small vineyard paddocks for one to three days, while chickens scratch manure into the organic ground cover. After grazing the vineyards, the animals move into the estate’s woodland to reduce fire fuel. Hanzell later obtained CCOF organic certification in 2021, another documented milestone in the estate’s farming transition.
identity_note: The catalog is consistent with Hanzell estate Pinot Noir but identifies neither vintage nor precise release. Hanzell distinguishes Heritage Pinot Noir from Ambassador’s 1953 Vineyard Pinot Noir. This producer-level account does not establish the farming practices or winemaker for this bottle.

title: From Fittings to First Harvest
anecdote:
Justin Ennis joined Freestone as its dedicated winery neared completion and took on the practical job of equipping the cellar, from tanks down to fittings. In his retrospective account, his first Freestone season meant preparing a nearly finished building to receive grapes, not simply stepping into an established cellar.

The winery received its first harvest in early September 2007. Joseph Phelps’s estate history also marks 2007 as the first production of the Pastorale and Quarter Moon single-vineyard wines, alongside the existing Freestone Vineyards bottlings—a new chapter for the producer’s Freestone program.
identity_note: The abbreviated catalog name likely denotes Freestone Vineyards Pinot Noir but does not exclude Pastorale or Quarter Moon. Vintage is unknown. This producer-level story does not establish who made the cataloged bottle; Ennis’s documented 2022 winemaker title should not be assumed for 2007.

title: From Growers to Family Winery
anecdote:
Arturo and Deborah Keller began planting Chardonnay in 1989 after advisers recommended it for their cold site: if the grapes failed to ripen sufficiently, sparkling wine offered a possible fallback. The family initially sold its Chardonnay to Rombauer rather than making wine under its own name.

The Kellers later expanded into Pinot Noir and chose to become producers themselves. Arturo invited their daughter Ana into that transition; she joined the venture in 1998. Keller Estate dates its first vintage to 2000, marking the move from supplying another winery to releasing the family’s own wines.
identity_note: Producer history only: the catalog identifies neither La Cruz nor El Coro Pinot Noir, and the vintage is unknown. Ana’s documented role is estate leadership, not necessarily hands-on winemaking for this bottle.

title: From Growers to Estate
anecdote:
Paul Hobbs approached growers Larry Hyde and Richard Dinner in 1991 to purchase five tons of Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Cabernet Sauvignon. Their grapes became his winery’s debut releases, giving the founding winemaker a start built on purchased fruit and relationships with independent growers.

In 1998, Hobbs established Katherine Lindsay Estate in Sebastopol to cultivate his own vineyard; its first harvest followed in 2003. The winery now identifies this Russian River Valley estate as its home site and documents Pinot Noir plantings there—a concrete step from buying grapes toward growing them.
identity_note: The abbreviated catalog name does not distinguish the Russian River Valley appellation Pinot Noir from a vineyard-designated bottling. Vintage is unknown; this producer-level story does not establish this bottle’s vineyard sources.

title: Learning the Blocks
anecdote:
Thomas Savre joined Lingua Franca as its first employee in May 2015 and studied how the young estate’s vineyard blocks developed differently. In a 2020 interview, he linked those observations to separately identified wines, associating The Plow with the estate’s highest blocks, shallow soils and steep slope.

The selection later widened: the 2022 technical sheet records The Plow as principally drawn from Block 1, with Blocks 3, 6 and 4 entering the final cuvée for the first time. Savre oversaw winemaking and farming; the sheet does not credit him alone with that change.
identity_note: The catalog matches The Plow, but its vintage is unknown. This story concerns documented estate-era releases, not necessarily this bottle: the winery identifies 2016 as the last vintage sourced from a neighboring vineyard. No vineyard source or block composition can be assigned to the undated bottle.

title: The Choice Behind Momtazi
anecdote:
Mark Vlossak approached Moe Momtazi in 2006 to ask about contracting Pinot Noir from Momtazi Vineyard. St. Innocent’s founder and continuing winemaker traced his interest in biodynamics to a 1998 trip to France, where he observed that the Burgundy and Alsace domaines he most admired farmed that way.

Momtazi offered a Demeter-certified biodynamic vineyard, and St. Innocent made its first Momtazi Vineyard vintage in 2006. That sourcing decision established this vineyard-designated Pinot Noir; Vlossak later recounted the French influence and his approach to Moe in the winery’s 2014 technical sheet.
identity_note: Vintage unknown: the catalog name supplies no year. The 2014 technical sheet documents the sourcing story, not the vintage of this bottle.

title: Two Parcels, Then a Wait
anecdote:
Hannes Storm identified two small vineyard parcels after twelve vintages working with Pinot Noir and Chardonnay in Hemel-en-Aarde. One lay in Hemel-en-Aarde Valley, the other in Upper Hemel-en-Aarde Valley; both were planted to Pinot Noir in 2008, laying the groundwork for Storm Wines.

Those plantings led to the producer’s first vintage in 2012. Storm then held the wines for eighteen months in bottle before releasing them in August 2014. Today, Hannes and Nathalia Storm are the husband-and-wife team behind a portfolio that also includes Ridge Pinot Noir.
identity_note: Storm Wines is verified, but Ridge Pinot Noir is only a provisional cuvée match: the catalog omits the cuvée name. Vintage unknown. This producer-level story concerns the original Valley and Upper Valley parcels, not Ridge’s planting or first harvest.

title: The Undeclared Year
anecdote:
Régis Camus privately assembled a small quantity of Rare from the 1997 wines after management saw no need to produce Rare and declared no vintage. He bottled it exclusively in magnums, a first for the house according to Rare’s account.

The bottles stayed in Camus’s private cellar for more than twenty years before the experiment became Rare Le Secret, a separate exceptional edition. His decision preserved wines from a year management had passed over; Rare announced his retirement and handover to Émilien Boutillat in April 2022.
identity_note: Producer-level story, not identification as Le Secret or the 1997 vintage. Piper-Heidsieck is the historic attribution; Rare became a standalone maison in 2018. The catalog identifies neither vintage nor white versus rosé, and its Meunier listing remains unverified. Camus is a historical maker; responsibility for this bottle cannot be assigned.

title: A Vineyard Becomes Poggio Valente
anecdote:
Elisabetta Geppetti bought the Poggio Valente vineyard near Pereta in 1996, beginning a project focused on Sangiovese at Fattoria Le Pupille. Her acquisition was the starting point for the named wine: the estate records Poggio Valente’s first vintage as 1997, the year after the purchase.

The vineyard project continued beyond that first release. In its current account of Poggio Valente, Le Pupille records planting two additional parcels over subsequent years. Those additions extend the story from Geppetti’s original purchase to the continued development of the vineyard behind this cuvée.
identity_note: The catalog names Fattoria La Pupille; the matched producer is Fattoria Le Pupille. Vintage is unknown. The current Toscana Rosso IGT designation and the 2013 sheet’s Morellino di Scansano DOCG Riserva designation are not assigned to this bottle.

title: A Cellar Master's Handover
anecdote:
Pol Roger appointed Damien Cambres cellar master on April 2, 2018, following Dominique Petit’s retirement after 19 years at the house. Before leaving, Petit worked to pass the family-owned producer’s winemaking knowledge and philosophy to his successor: a deliberate handover rather than simply a change of names.

Cambres brought roughly two decades of Champagne cooperative experience. At Feuillatte, he had progressed from laboratory work into production responsibilities between 1997 and 2012; he later became production manager, then general manager, at Gouttes d’Or Union before taking responsibility for Pol Roger’s cellar.
identity_note: Producer-level story; the unspecified vintage cannot be attributed to either cellar master. Pol Roger specifies Pinot Noir and Chardonnay only, conflicting with the catalog’s Meunier listing; exact proportions are undisclosed. The supplied name does not establish Édition Vinothèque.

title: Selected Twice for Louise
anecdote:
Pommery assigned 200 dedicated pickers to separately marked parcels in Avize, Cramant and Aÿ for Cuvée Louise, according to its Rosé 2003 sheet. The team consisted principally of experienced older workers, making grape selection a task for a dedicated group rather than the wider harvest workforce.

The house continued that selection at the press: from each 4,000 kilograms of grapes, it retained only 1,800 litres from the first two extractions. This deliberately restricted the quantity of juice admitted to Cuvée Louise, extending the vineyard team’s selection into the cellar.
identity_note: The catalog vintage is unknown; these practices are documented in the Rosé 2003 sheet, not established for this bottle. The sheet does not attribute the decisions to an individual. The catalog’s Meunier listing remains unverified.

title: Replanting After Phylloxera
anecdote:
The Latour family bought the Corton Grancey winery, château and vineyards in 1891, taking on holdings where phylloxera had destroyed approximately two-thirds of the vines. Rather than abandon the damaged vineyards, the family replanted them, making a consequential change in what they grew.

Louis Latour, identified in the house history as the fifth of that name, chose Chardonnay for vineyards south of Corton instead of restoring the earlier plantings. The producer links that decision to the creation of its Corton-Charlemagne white wine: a separate chapter in the history of the house that makes this Pouilly-Fuissé.
identity_note: The catalog identifies standard Pouilly-Fuissé, not Premier Cru; vintage unknown. This story concerns the producer’s Corton holdings, not the vineyards supplying this cuvée. Official accounts differ on the displaced varieties, so they are not specified.

title: The Brothers Behind Prestige
anecdote:
Jean-Etienne and François Matton created Prestige within their family’s Minuty business. The third-generation brothers also reconsidered the estate’s winemaking process and introduced modern technical tools. Minuty dates their cuvée’s introduction to more than 25 years ago, without giving a precise launch year.

For Prestige, Minuty combines selected grapes from Provence with fruit from selected estate parcels. That production model gives a concrete shape to the brothers’ creation: a wine drawing on both estate fruit and grapes selected elsewhere in Provence, rather than estate parcels alone.
identity_note: The cuvée is verified, but the vintage is unknown. The current producer listing includes Rolle alongside the catalog’s Grenache/Cinsault/Syrah; it cannot establish this bottle’s blend.

title: Rustico’s Change of Method
anecdote:
Primo Franco joined his father in the Nino Franco cellar in 1971 after graduating from Conegliano’s enology school, focusing exclusively on Prosecco. Rustico was already part of the estate’s production in the 1970s, made as col fondo, with its lees retained.

In 1979, while Primo was working alongside his father, Nino Franco changed Rustico to the Charmat method. The estate’s current technical description specifies second fermentation in a pressurized tank: a documented change to an existing cuvée, rather than the introduction of a new label.
identity_note: No vintage or release is identified. The current producer listing identifies Rustico as Valdobbiadene Prosecco Superiore DOCG Brut; the supplied earlier DOC Treviso identity remains unresolved for this catalog bottle. The sources do not identify Primo as the sole decision-maker behind the 1979 change.

title: Keeping the Style, Changing Classification
anecdote:
Dal Forno Romano chose to keep its established sweet-wine style rather than alter it to meet appellation requirements. From the 2003 vintage, the wine’s characteristics were no longer considered compliant with Recioto della Valpolicella DOC rules, and the winery accepted IGT classification instead.

The estate named the resulting wine Vigna Seré, after a locality containing its vineyards, under the Veneto IGT designation. That change marks a documented turning point in the Recioto lineage of the estate Romano Dal Forno founded in 1983, when he began making wine from family vineyards.
identity_note: The catalog vintage is unknown. Its Recioto identity must not be replaced with the later Vigna Seré designation. The classification decision is attributed to the winery, not specifically to Romano or Marco.

title: From Merchant to Vineyard Owner
anecdote:
Roberto Anselmi gradually closed his family’s wine-merchant operation, renting and then buying hillside vineyards. His father Almerino had founded the company in 1948 to bottle and sell purchased wines; Roberto chose instead to rebuild a vineyard property after his grandfather had been forced to sell his land amid wartime economic disruption.

In his professional biography, Roberto describes denser planting, less-productive Garganega selections and fewer bunches. He also names the passito I Capitelli among his wines, linking this cuvée to the vineyard-owning estate he built rather than the purchased-wine business he left behind.
identity_note: No vintage is supplied. The catalog’s Recioto di Soave designation remains unverified; the current producer sheet lists Goldtraminer and Garganega, so Garganega-only composition is also unverified. Sources disagree on Roberto’s return date, and neither identifies who made this undated bottle.

title: A Visit Becomes a Handover
anecdote:
Peter Skaff accompanied his father, Naji, on a wine-related visit to Ammiq in 2008 while still a university student. He later identified that visit as the turning point that led him to study oenology and viticulture in France, followed by internships and wine-consultancy work in New Zealand and the United States.

Peter returned to Lebanon in mid-2016 to gradually take over production from Naji; 2017 became his first vintage entirely under his direction. His sister Aida also returned from marketing work in London to help turn their father’s hobby label into a commercial family enterprise.
identity_note: Reserve Ammiq is the probable producer, but its listed Chardonnay is not verified as the catalog’s “Reserve Ammiq Blanc.” This story is producer-level only. Vintage is unknown, so the bottle cannot be attributed to Peter rather than Naji.

sources.title: Profiling new Lebanese wines – Executive Magazine

title: An Apprenticeship That Changed Course
anecdote:
Cornelius Dönnhoff chose an apprenticeship with Joachim Heger in Baden at eighteen, despite initially not wanting to become a winegrower. Growing up, he had associated his father’s work with constant demands—even his September birthday fell under harvest’s shadow. A planned year away became three and a half.

That apprenticeship changed his direction: seeing how vineyard work, cellar work and the business fitted together made winemaking a future he could choose. Cornelius took responsibility for Dönnhoff’s cellar in 2007; his father, Helmut, transferred ownership to him in 2015.
identity_note: The producer is verified as Weingut Dönnhoff. The catalog name does not identify an exact bottling, distinguish dry from off-dry Riesling, or establish a vintage; this story concerns the producer.

title: A Growing Cellar of Barrels
anecdote:
Von Winning adopted spontaneous fermentation in wooden barrels in 2008, a year after Stephan Attmann took over management. In his VDP interview, Attmann also describes bottling by gravity rather than pumps whenever possible, adding another concrete choice to the estate’s cellar approach.

The barrel work continued to evolve. In a 2020 interview, colleague Andreas Hütwohl described the team refining fermentation and maturation in oak while building a broader collection of barrels in different sizes and ages. Wood was not simply a one-time change, but an ongoing part of the team’s work.
identity_note: The Kirchenstück GG identity is verified, but the catalog vintage is unknown. The supplied 2023 technical sheet documents spontaneous barrel fermentation for that vintage only. Attmann is managing director; the VDP separately identifies Kurt Rathgeber as cellarmaster.

title: Bringing Montaña Back to Market
anecdote:
Román Montaña consolidated the family business in 1920, supplying the vineyard component of an established Rioja house whose cellars lay beneath Haro. Nearly a century later, the estate, directed by his grandson Óscar Montaña, announced plans to bring the family surname back to market.

The launch was scheduled for September 2015, with Reserva 2011 explicitly included alongside Tinto and Crianza. The estate also planned to reserve the Familia Montaña designation for selected single-site bottlings and exceptional vintages, distinguishing those wines from the broader Montaña range.
identity_note: Matched to Montaña Reserva by Familia Montaña S.L. The catalog gives no vintage; neither 2011 nor 2017 can be assigned. Rioja Alta is not confirmed as the vineyard origin of this unidentified release.

title: A Reserva Before a Winery
anecdote:
Luis Valentín and Carmen Enciso founded Valenciso in 1998, after fifteen years working together in winery management. With little money for premises, they partnered with growers, including one with winemaking facilities, and chose to begin with just one wine: a Reserva.

Their early operation stretched across Rioja towns: offices occupied the second floor of Enciso’s house, while production, maturation, bottling and bottle storage happened elsewhere. They established their own winery in Ollauri in 2003, bringing a permanent home to the project begun around that original Reserva.
identity_note: Vintage unknown. The producer identifies documented Reserva examples as 100% Tempranillo, unlike the catalog’s blend designation. This founding history does not establish current ownership or winemaking roles; Iberian now lists Valenciso among its wineries.

title: A Farmhouse and a Spring
anecdote:
Paolo Manzone and his wife, Luisella, chose in 1999 to establish their own agricultural business after his years as a wine consultant. They renovated the old farmhouse at Serralunga d’Alba, where the house and Meriame vineyards had belonged to Luisella’s family for generations.

Luisella’s grandparents had sold their grapes to others, and the house had stood empty for more than 25 years. The couple restored it for guests and expanded the adjoining cellar, incorporating an existing spring into the basement to provide natural humidity.
identity_note: The catalog matches Paolo Manzone’s Roero Arneis DOCG “Reysú”; vintage unknown. This story concerns the producer’s estate renovation, not the Arneis vineyard or its production.

title: A Harvest Redirected to Rosso
anecdote:
Canalicchio di Sopra changed its harvest plan in 2014. In reporting preserved by the estate, Francesco Ripaccioli described a prolonged harvest: the team removed unhealthy grapes in mid-September, then picked 80% of the remaining fruit for Rosso on September 25.

Brunello picking began on October 5, selecting only the smallest, most concentrated bunches. A separate contemporary review records the result for the 2014 Rosso di Montalcino: substantial fruit potentially destined for Brunello went into Rosso instead, increasing production of this cuvée that year.
identity_note: The catalog identifies no vintage. This story concerns the documented 2014 Rosso, not necessarily the wine offered. Harvest details come from reporting retained in the producer’s archive.

title: Old Vines, Rosso First
anecdote:
Casanova di Neri purchased Tocci, a seven-hectare old-vine vineyard in southeastern Montalcino, in 2018. By then, Giacomo Neri was working alongside sons Giovanni and Gianlorenzo, who had joined the family estate in 2012 and 2017 respectively. The estate connects that acquisition and its first harvest to the new Giovanni Neri wines.

The project reached the market first as Rosso: Giovanni Neri Rosso di Montalcino 2018 was released in 2020, three years before the corresponding Brunello’s debut. The estate describes this Rosso as coming mainly, not exclusively, from an older vineyard.
identity_note: Catalog vintage unknown; 2018 refers to the cuvée’s first harvest, not the supplied bottle. Founder Giovanni Neri is the namesake, distinct from his grandson Giovanni, who has a production role.
