title: Studying Light, Developing Protection
anecdote:
Caroline Fiot researched light-strike affecting Ruinart Blanc de Blancs while working on the house’s winemaking team. She joined in 2016 under Frédéric Panaïotis, taking part in the tasting committee and supervising harvest fermentations. Ruinart also credits her with contributing to the creation of its Second Skin case.

That packaging project brought Ruinart together with manufacturers Pusterla 1880 and James Cropper for two years of research and development before its 2020 introduction. The house describes the case for Blanc de Blancs as protection against light exposure that can stay around the bottle until serving.
identity_note: Vintage unknown; the catalog does not confirm Second Skin packaging. Fiot became cellar master on January 1, 2026, but the sources do not identify who oversaw this undated bottle’s production.

title: Changing the Vineyard Work
anecdote:
Domaine Yves Martin stopped using herbicides and made working the soil a priority in its family vineyards at Chavignol. The estate, also documented as Domaine Pierre Martin, describes a practical challenge behind that work: its steep vineyards are difficult to mechanize, so most operations are carried out by hand.

Pierre Martin, Yves’s son, is the documented winemaker. A technical sheet for the estate’s 2019 Sancerre Chavignol records its conversion to organic viticulture, while the domaine describes choosing treatments according to weather and disease pressure rather than applying them indiscriminately.
identity_note: Vintage unknown. The 2019 sheet does not establish this bottle’s farming status or completed organic certification. Succession dates conflict; the herbicide decision is not dated or attributed solely to Pierre.

title: A Closer Look at Each Parcel
anecdote:
Domaine Hubert Brochard appointed Rodrigo Zamorano to lead the estate and its winemaking in December 2022. The team then worked with the Bureau Interprofessionnel des Vins du Centre-Loire, drilling soil profiles across the vineyard to understand its individual sites more precisely.

That parcel-by-parcel reassessment extended into the cellar, with separate vinification in small tanks and maturation vessels chosen case by case. The estate introduced amphorae in 2023 and placed Les Monts Damnés in its reworked Les Parcellaires collection, connecting this hillside wine to the team's renewed attention to individual parcels.
identity_note: The estate's La Côte des Monts Damnés and Les Monts Damnés names support the catalog match. No vintage is supplied; this post-2022 producer story does not establish Zamorano's involvement or a maturation method for the particular bottle.

title: From Leadership to Cellar Practice
anecdote:
Catherine Corbeau-Mellot took over Joseph Mellot in 2005 after her husband Alexandre’s death, having joined the business in 1987 to work on commercial and export development. As estate leader, she initiated the cellar’s ISO 14001 environmental certification in 2009, followed by High Environmental Value certification in 2019.

The estate describes the practical work behind that environmental program: limiting natural-resource use and sorting, recycling or recovering glass, plastics, wood, paper, cardboard and corks. La Chatellenie’s archived 2017 technical sheet records the ISO certification, connecting this cuvée to the estate’s documented environmental work.
identity_note: Vintage unknown; the 2017 sheet verifies the cuvée, not this catalog entry’s vintage or certification status. Catherine’s documented role is estate leadership, not hands-on vinification.

title: From Dijon to Foucher
anecdote:
Marc Vappereau joined Maison Foucher in 2001, working alongside Jacky Foucher, the founder’s grandson. Trained in oenology in Dijon, he had worked in Mercurey, Melbourne and London before settling in Sancerre—a path that brought him into the family house before he took its helm in 2013.

His subsequent work includes discovering vineyard sites and selecting parcel-specific cuvées. Maison Foucher places its Classiques range under Vappereau’s work, and lists white Sancerre Le Mont within that range: a documented connection between his leadership and this wine’s place in the portfolio.
identity_note: The Sauvignon Blanc designation supports the white Le Mont match; the house also uses Le Mont for red and rosé Sancerre. Vintage unknown. Sources establish Vappereau’s producer-level role, not that he created this cuvée or made this particular bottle.

title: Quality Before Quantity
anecdote:
Remoissenet Père et Fils pays its grape suppliers according to quality rather than quantity, adding bonuses for exceptional fruit. That purchasing decision rewards growers for what they deliver, not simply how much. The team also uses three sorting tables at harvest, extending selection beyond the buying agreement.

For the documented 2017 Grand Clos Rousseau, Remoissenet bought fruit from a single grower’s parcel but sent its own team to harvest it. Grapes were sorted in the vineyard and again in the cellar; the technical sheet credits Claudie Jobard as winemaker.
identity_note: The catalog vintage is unknown. The 2017 technical sheet confirms the cuvée’s identity and documents that release only; the producer’s purchasing policy is not attributed to Jobard personally.

title: Two Trades, One Basement Barrel
anecdote:
Duncan Arnot Meyers and Nathan Lee Roberts founded Arnot-Roberts in 2001 with one barrel of wine made in their basement. They had grown up together in Napa Valley but arrived at the partnership through different trades: Duncan worked in Napa and Sonoma wineries, while Nathan worked alongside his father as an oak-barrel cooper.

The partners then expanded gradually, sourcing grapes from vineyards across California rather than beginning with an estate vineyard. Single-vineyard wines became the core of their production, carrying that one-barrel beginning into a broader vineyard-sourcing operation.
identity_note: Producer matched; exact Sauvignon Blanc cuvée unresolved and vintage unknown. The catalog’s Sonoma County designation conflicts with the documented Randle Hill (Yorkville Highlands) and Ascona (Santa Cruz Mountains) bottlings. This story is producer-level history, not the origin of either Sauvignon Blanc.

title: An Unconventional Hire
anecdote:
Fred Schrader recruited Thomas Rivers Brown in 2000 after meeting him while Brown was working at a local wine shop. Brown had begun his Napa winemaking career at Turley Cellars, but had not yet made his first Cabernet Sauvignon when Schrader brought him onto the team.

That appointment connects to this white wine through a later, documented credit: Schrader named Brown as winemaker for the inaugural 2022 Double Diamond Napa Valley Sauvignon Blanc. Double Diamond’s team biography also places both vineyard management and winemaking under his oversight.
identity_note: The catalog identifies no vintage; 2022 is cited only as the documented inaugural release, not as the year of this bottle.

title: From Biotechnology to Sinegal
anecdote:
Ryan Knoth left biotechnology to pursue wine after finding little fulfillment in his work. With support from his wife and family, he changed careers; his subsequent cellar experience included working alongside Danielle Cyrot at St. Clement, Fredrik Johansson at Staglin Family Vineyard and Philippe Melka at Gandona.

By November 2018, Knoth was Sinegal Estate’s winemaker. His studies in biology and chemistry at Cal Poly informed his approach to vineyard and cellar decisions, combining technology with established winemaking practices. Sinegal’s technical sheet also names him as winemaker for its 2018 Sauvignon Blanc.
identity_note: The catalog vintage is unknown. Knoth’s documented connection to the 2018 Sauvignon Blanc does not establish that he made the unidentified catalog vintage. This is Sinegal Estate Sauvignon Blanc, not DETAILS by Sinegal.

title: Small Ferments, Separate Paths
anecdote:
Craggy Range kept small fermentations inside its large winery. In a 2022 interview, Ben Tombs described separate paths for its Sauvignon Blanc: most fruit was machine-picked and handled in closed, inert presses, while a hand-picked portion fermented in puncheons or foudres. The team maintained distinct components rather than one uniform stream.

That approach also appears in the estate’s account of Te Muna Sauvignon Blanc: vineyard blocks receive individual treatment, and Tombs blends the resulting components. He joined Craggy Range in 2021 and became chief winemaker in November 2023.
identity_note: Vintage unknown. This producer-level account does not establish that Tombs made the catalog bottle or that the 2022 practices apply unchanged to its release.

title: Farming for Sea Spray
anecdote:
Sea Smoke developed Sea Spray as an estate Blanc de Noirs, drawing on its Pinot Noir work and taking grower Champagne as a model. Its first vintage was 2008, the same year Don Schroeder became winemaker after joining the estate as cellarmaster in 2003.

Schroeder’s team then worked to identify the estate’s most suitable Pinot Noir blocks specifically for Sea Spray and tailored their farming accordingly. The sparkling project thus extended into vineyard decisions, with blocks selected and farmed for this cuvée rather than treated simply as another source of still Pinot Noir.
identity_note: Sea Spray is sparkling Blanc de Noirs, not a still Pinot Noir cuvée. The catalog identifies no vintage; 2008 is the project's first vintage, not an identification of this bottle.

title: From Abandoned Vines to Whites
anecdote:
Arianna Occhipinti rented an abandoned hectare beside her parents’ country house after university and restored it as she learned to grow grapes. Her first independent vintage, in 2004, began with academic knowledge but little vineyard experience. That hectare yielded 2,000 bottles each of Frappato and Nero d’Avola; she then planted around the original plot.

Her expansion also brought white grapes into the project. In a 2011 interview, she recalled planting Albanello and Muscat six years earlier, noting how little Albanello was then produced. Those varieties match the Albanello and Moscato di Alessandria documented for SP68 Bianco today.
identity_note: Vintage unknown. The interview does not identify the white planting as SP68 Bianco’s exclusive source or establish its first release year.

title: From Land Search to Syrah
anecdote:
Drew and Laurie Duncan began searching for vineyard land in the early 2000s, bought their Sta. Rita Hills property in 2012 and started planting the following year. Donnachadh’s founders and proprietors thus became growers after a search that stretched across years.

The Duncans also met Ernst Storm at a wine dinner in Santa Barbara; the estate now names him as its winemaker. Their first Syrah harvest came in 2016, and the documented 2021 Estate Syrah names Storm as winemaker, connecting that partnership directly to this cuvée.
identity_note: The catalog matches Donnachadh Family Wines’ Estate Syrah. Its vintage is unknown; the 2021 technical sheet verifies the cuvée and that bottling’s winemaker, not the year of this entry.

title: Two Generations, One Cask Project
anecdote:
Peter Symington selected wines from Warre’s Quinta da Cavadinha’s 1995 harvest, adding wine from Quinta do Retiro, for what became Otima Colheita 1995. That same year, his son Charles joined the family company and began an apprenticeship under Peter, then Head Winemaker.

After Peter retired in 2009, Charles took responsibility for monitoring the selected 1995 wine as it continued ageing in seasoned oak casks. He later chose wines for bottling from 2018, carrying his father’s selection forward through a second generation of decisions within Warre’s Otima range.
identity_note: Producer/range context: this story concerns Otima Colheita 1995, not necessarily the catalog bottle. The catalog specifies neither an age designation nor a harvest year; its exact release and vintage remain unknown.

title: Replanting and Rebuilding Noval
anecdote:
Christian Seely appointed António Agrellos technical director after becoming Quinta do Noval’s managing director in 1993. Following AXA Millésimes’ acquisition that year, the two undertook a joint programme of vineyard replanting and estate renovation. During the 1990s, around 100 hectares were replanted, with pruning methods adapted to individual parcels.

The rebuilding also reached beyond the vineyards: a new bottling line and warehouse at Alijó were completed in 1997. According to Noval’s history, this made the estate the first traditional Port shipper to centralise all its activities in the Douro Valley.
identity_note: Producer confirmed; the catalog does not distinguish Fine Tawny, Tawny Reserve or an age-designated Tawny. No vintage is specified. This story concerns the producer, not a verified cuvée or its blender. António Agrellos retired in 2018 and was succeeded by Carlos Agrellos.

title: From Family Table to Release
anecdote:
Will Harlan spent several years persuading his family and their winegrowing team to share The Mascot beyond their own table. It began as an unnamed, unlabeled wine poured for family and close friends, drawn from younger vines at Harlan Estate, BOND and Promontory.

His persistence led to a named, labeled release beginning with the 2008 vintage; the producer dates its public introduction to 2013. Will also recalls personally labeling a few 2007 bottles—a small exception before the first release, and a hands-on detail in the founder’s account.
identity_note: The producer identifies The Mascot as Napa Valley Cabernet Sauvignon, rather than the catalog’s Bordeaux-Style Red Blend. No vintage is specified. Will Harlan is the founder; Cory Empting is the winemaker.

title: The Experiment Became Tignanello
anecdote:
Piero Antinori recruited Bordeaux consultant Émile Peynaud after visiting Bordeaux in the late 1960s in search of solutions for his business. Experiments involving Giacomo Tachis produced Tignanello, but selling it as table wine rather than Chianti Classico initially gave Piero pause.

Journalist Luigi Veronelli encouraged him to use the vineyard’s name. Antinori’s archive records the change: the 1970 Chianti Classico Riserva Vigneto Tignanello became Tignanello, a Tuscan table wine, in 1971. That vintage reached the market in 1974; white grapes were eliminated with the 1975 vintage.
identity_note: The catalog gives no vintage. Dates and classifications describe the cuvée’s documented development, not the unidentified bottle’s vintage or classification.

title: Rebuilding Il Borro’s Vineyards
anecdote:
Salvatore Ferragamo joined Il Borro’s restoration in 1993, with particular attention to renewing wine production. Ferruccio’s son, he holds responsibility for the estate’s winemaking and hospitality. In 1995, father and son decided to revive its winemaking tradition.

Salvatore’s vineyard-renewal project began with studying the estate’s soils and microclimate, recovering historic vineyards and introducing additional varieties. At producer level, one concrete outcome was the flagship Il Borro: geological study preceded planting Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon and Syrah in selected soils, establishing the blend for that bottling.
identity_note: Producer identified; cuvée unresolved. The catalog’s Sangiovese-led description conflicts with the official flagship blend of Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon and Syrah. This story is producer-level, not an identification of the catalog bottling. Vintage unspecified.

title: From Architecture to the Cellar
anecdote:
Barbara Widmer joined her first Brancaia harvest in 1993 while studying architecture—a turning point toward winemaking. In 1994, she took a year-long internship at Domaine des Balisiers, an organic producer in Geneva, then began studying oenology at Wädenswil in 1995.

She returned to Brancaia as a qualified oenologist in 1998, when her parents entrusted her with running the estate. That year also brought completion of the Radda cellar, allowing Brancaia to vinify and mature its wines independently for the first time. TRE’s first production followed in 2000.
identity_note: Vintage unknown. This is a producer-level career story; the sources do not establish that Widmer’s architecture studies or apprenticeship prompted TRE’s creation.

title: Keeping Half for Later
anecdote:
Emidio Pepe chose to hold bottles back rather than sell his entire production, making ageing central to his work with both Trebbiano and Montepulciano d’Abruzzo. For the winery’s founder, keeping wine in the cellar was part of the project, not simply a way to store unsold bottles.

The estate says it retains at least half its production, with the family deciding when each vintage is ready for release. Older bottles leave in small quantities as younger wines enter storage, keeping the cellar archive active across successive harvests.
identity_note: Vintage unknown. The catalog does not establish this bottle’s release history or identify it as Selezione Vecchie Vigne; it should not be assumed to be an older cellar release or personally vinified by Emidio.

title: Replanting From Their Oldest Vines
anecdote:
Cristiana and Antonio Tiberio chose to uproot the international varieties their father, Riccardo, had planted and replace them with Pecorino and Trebbiano Abruzzese. The siblings took over the estate in 2008; Cristiana handles winemaking and Antonio manages the vineyards. Their decision redirected part of their father’s planting program toward indigenous grapes.

For those replacements, they used massal selections from their own oldest vines rather than clonal selections. Riccardo had established the estate around an old Trebbiano Abruzzese vineyard he bought in 2000; the next generation made older estate vines the source for its new plantings.
identity_note: The catalog matches Tiberio’s regular Trebbiano d’Abruzzo DOP, not Fonte Canale. Vintage unknown. This estate-level story does not establish that replacement-planting fruit entered this bottling.

title: Pausing the Harvest
anecdote:
Vega Sicilia’s vineyard and cellar team revised its harvest plans for Valbuena 5º in 2020 after heavy rain. Rather than rely on earlier expectations, they monitored the vineyard, tasted grapes and analysed them to track concentration after the rainfall.

When more rain arrived during picking, the team interrupted the harvest so it could collect dry, healthy grapes. That season also required new COVID-protection measures; the estate reported that adapting to these conditions strengthened team spirit. The documented response combined close checks on the fruit with changes to how the team worked.
identity_note: The catalog matches Valbuena 5º, but its vintage is unknown; five refers to the ageing cycle. The 2020 episode is producer context, not the established history of this bottle. Harvest decisions are credited to the team, not personally to Gonzalo Iturriaga.

title: An Invitation Became a Partnership
anecdote:
Chris Ringland accepted importer Jorge Ordóñez’s invitation to explore winemaking projects in Spain in 2001. Already consulting in Italy and California, he spent roughly two weeks visiting Spanish vineyards and meeting winemakers. That exploratory trip led him to become a consultant, and later a partner, at Alto Moncayo.

The relationship also gave Ringland access to wine allocations for Australia. He chose to hold those wines for two additional years in bottle before offering them: a concrete release decision that followed his move from visiting consultant to producer partner.
identity_note: Veraton is verified as an Alto Moncayo cuvée; vintage unknown. Ringland’s documented role is historical consultant and partner, not sole or current winemaker. His Australian allocation policy is not established for this particular bottle.

title: From Restoration to Estate Responsibility
anecdote:
Federica Mascheroni Stianti trained in art restoration before joining her family’s wine business. She completed a master’s in Restoration and Conservation of Artistic Heritage, then gained practical knowledge of viticulture and enology at Falesco in Umbria with Riccardo Cotarella.

In May 2007, her father Carlo bought the Prelius estate for her. Federica dates her full-time commitment to wine to 2010, with responsibilities including Prelius–Castelprile in Maremma. That estate produces Prelius Vermentino; its technical sheet names Castelprile di Federica Mascheroni Stianti as the producer.
identity_note: The catalog’s Volpaia attribution matches its portfolio estate Castelprile. Federica is documented as proprietor and family-business representative, not as this cuvée’s hands-on winemaker. Catalog vintage is unknown; the 2022 technical sheet establishes identity only.

title: Learning the Yellow Label Blend
anecdote:
Didier Mariotti spent four months learning from outgoing Veuve Clicquot cellar master Dominique Demarville. The handover covered Yellow Label’s blend, the reserve collection and decisions about which wines to retain each year. Mariotti also learned the house’s tasting vocabulary and grading system, assessing wines for Clicquot’s cuvées rather than his own preferences.

Today, the house describes an eight-oenologist committee led by Mariotti tasting and categorizing more than 1,000 wines between November and March. Their decisions assign wines to blends, reserves, potential vintage wines or rejection: the selection work behind the cellar master’s role.
identity_note: Yellow Label is a non-vintage cuvée. No release or lot is identified, so Mariotti’s supervision of this particular bottle cannot be established.

title: Back to His Training Ground
anecdote:
Emiliano Falsini returned to Villa Montepaldi’s cellar after studying at the estate and graduating in 1999. His professional return brought him back to the place where he had trained: a working agricultural estate that also carries out experimental and scientific research for the University of Florence.

By 2019, Falsini was documented as Montepaldi’s responsible oenologist, working alongside Nicola Menditto, the estate’s director and in-house oenologist. The former student had become part of its cellar team—not its sole identified maker—bringing his career back into the estate’s production work.
identity_note: The catalog matches Villa Montepaldi’s Il Decano, also listed as Decano. Vintage unknown. This producer-level story documents Falsini’s role in 2019, not his current position, creation of the cuvée, or responsibility for the unspecified bottle.

title: A White Wine Joins the Reds
anecdote:
Lynn and Ron Penner-Ash established Penner-Ash Wine Cellars in 1998, initially producing small quantities of Pinot Noir and Syrah. Lynn was the founding winemaker; the winery’s early production centered on those two reds before Viognier joined the range.

The team made its first bottling of Viognier in 2000, crediting the addition to its enthusiasm for Viognier fruit encountered in the vineyards. The winery tells this as a collective decision, without naming one person as the instigator of that first white-wine bottling.
identity_note: Producer and wine match. Vintage is unknown. Official sources name the wine Oregon Viognier; the catalog’s narrower Rogue Valley designation is unconfirmed for this unidentified release. The historical story does not establish who made this bottle.

title: Bernard Gros’s Interrupted Apprenticeship
anecdote:
Bernard Gros joined his aunt Colette and uncle Gustave at Domaine Gros Frère et Sœur in 1980 to learn winegrowing. Four years later, Gustave’s premature death changed the course of that apprenticeship: Colette formed a partnership with Bernard, who was then just 22.

The estate credits Bernard with more than thirty years of restructuring and replanting its vineyards, giving his role a practical legacy beyond the family name. Its account records a handover to his children, Élodie and Vincent, in 2010, carrying the family succession into another generation.
identity_note: The estate’s catalogue confirms Les Chaumes Premier Cru. Vintage unknown; this producer-level history does not establish who vinified the unidentified bottle.

title: Selection Starts in Winter
anecdote:
Grégory Patriat began selecting vineyard plots at winter’s end for Maison Jean-Claude Boisset, looking at orientation and favouring older, low-vigour vines. Appointed in 2002 to a role spanning vineyard and cellar, he specified cultivation without weedkillers, using ploughing or grass cover instead.

That work relied on a network: the maison’s press kit describes roughly 40 growers supplying it in an average year, with brokers helping match plots and working methods. In 2010, Patriat reported about 30 hectares under organic cultivation—a documented extension of his hands-on sourcing approach.
identity_note: Vintage unknown. This producer-level account does not establish that this bottle came from the organically cultivated hectares or was organically certified.

sources.title: Interview de Grégory Patriat des Vins de Jean-Claude Boisset

title: Continuity in the Cellar
anecdote:
Jean-Claude Neu oversaw day-to-day cellar work at Château d’Esclans when Sacha Lichine launched Whispering Angel in 2006. Trained in viticulture and oenology at Lycée Agricole de Hyères, Neu was then the estate’s only winemaking professional on staff, according to its account.

Neu worked first under founding consulting oenologist Patrick Léon, then alongside Patrick’s son Bertrand, technical director since 2011. The change in technical leadership did not replace the cellar master: Neu stayed in place, carrying forward the cellar standards and practices he had learned through working with the Léons.
identity_note: No vintage is identified in the catalog name; 2006 is the cuvée’s launch year, not this bottle’s vintage.

title: A Larger Role for Primitivo
anecdote:
Quivira’s team picked each variety for rosé rather than red wine in the 2022 Wine Creek Ranch release, with Hugh Chappelle credited as winemaker. They kept the lots separate through vinification. When late-August temperatures reached triple digits, much of the rosé fruit was already picked; the team removed sunburned and shriveled berries from what remained.
